\end{itemize}
Thus we have obtained 
\[
 \fint_{Q^0}\sum_{Q\in\mathcal{D}_j(Q^0)} 
    W_{r,Q}(A_{u,\delta}f)^q \operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_Q(x)\hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} x \lesssim \delta^{\gamma_u q} \fint_{R_j} G_j(x) \hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} x.
\]
Therefore
\begin{align*}
      \fint_{Q^0}&\sum_{Q\in \mathcal{D}(Q^0)}
 \ell(Q)^{m-m\beta q}\cdot  W_{r,Q}(A_{u,\delta}f)^q \operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_Q(x) \hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} x \\
& =\sum_{j=0}^\infty (2^{-j}\ell(Q^0))^{m-m\beta q}
\fint_{Q^0}\sum_{Q\in\mathcal{D}_j(Q^0)} 
    W_{r,Q}(A_{u,\delta}f)^q \operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_Q(x)\hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} x\\
    &\lesssim \sum_{j=0}^\infty \delta^{\gamma_u q} (2^{-j}\ell(Q^0))^{m-m\beta q}\fint_{R_j} G_j(x) \hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} x 
    \\
    & \lesssim \delta^{\gamma_u q}
\sum_{j=0}^{J-1} \fint_{R_j} (2^{-j}\ell(Q^0))^{m-m\beta q} G_j(x) \hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} x\\
 &\qquad\qquad+\delta^{\gamma_u q}
\fint_{3Q^0}\sum_{j=J}^\infty (2^{-j}\ell(Q^0))^{m-m\beta q} G_j(x) \hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} x
\\
&\leq \delta^{\gamma_u q}
\sum_{j=0}^{J-1} \fint_{R_j} \sum_{Q\in \mathcal{D}, Q\subseteq R_j}
 \ell(Q)^{m-m\beta q}\cdot  W_{r,Q}(f)^q \operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_Q(x) \hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} x\\
 &\qquad\qquad +\delta^{\gamma_u q}
\fint_{3Q^0}\sum_{Q\in \mathcal{D}, Q\subseteq 3Q^0}
 \ell(Q)^{m-m\beta q}\cdot  W_{r,Q}(f)^q \operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_Q(x)  \hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} x\\
&\lesssim \delta^{\gamma_u q}\cdot J\cdot  3 ^n\cdot \nrm{f}_{T^{\infty,q,r}_\beta}^q+
\delta^{\gamma_u q}\cdot 3^n\cdot \nrm{f}_{T^{\infty,q,r}_\beta}^q\\
&\lesssim \delta^{\gamma_u q} (1+\ln \delta)\nrm{f}_{T^{\infty,q,r}_\beta}^q,
\end{align*}
where we have used the dyadic Carleson bound on $f$ from Proposition~\ref{prop:dyadic} on each of the $3^n$ dyadic cubes that $R_j$ is the union of, for each $0\le j<J$, and
 on each of the dyadic cubes that make up $3Q^0$ for the second term.
Taking supremum over all $Q^0$ proves
$$
    \nrm{A_{u,\delta}f}_{T^{\infty,q,r}_{\beta}}
    \lesssim
    \delta^{\gamma_u} (1+\ln \delta)^{\frac1q}\,
    \nrm{f}_{T^{\infty,q,r}_{\beta}}.
$$

With this estimate we can argue as in Proposition~\ref{prop:modelops-whitneymixed} for $H^{\mathrm{w}}_{\boldsymbol{u}, \delta}$ and $H^{\mathrm{ca}}_{\boldsymbol{u}, \delta}$. 
Using again \eqref{eq:AudomHw} and replacing $u$ by $u_x$ so that  $\gamma_{u_x}=\gamma$, we immediately conclude that
$$
    \nrm{H^{\mathrm{w}}_{\boldsymbol{u}, \delta}f}_{T^{\infty,q,r}_{\beta}}
    \lesssim
    \nrm{A_{u_x,c^{-m}\delta}f}_{T^{\infty,q,r}_{\beta}}
    \lesssim
    \delta^{\gamma} (1+\ln \delta)^{\frac1q}\,
    \nrm{f}_{T^{\infty,q,r}_{\beta}}.
$$
For $H^{\mathrm{ca}}_{\boldsymbol{u}, \delta}f$, we only need to note the analogue of \eqref{eq:dilatedest} for $p=\infty$.
For fixed $(\tau,z) \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+$, we calculate 
\begin{align*}
    \int_0^\tau \fint_{B(z,\tau^{1/m})}
    & t^{-\beta q}
    \Bigl( \fint_{c^{m(k+1)}2^{-m}t}^{c^{mk}t}
    A_{u_x, c^{-m(k+2)}\delta} f(s,x)^r \hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} s\Bigr)^{q/r} \hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} x \hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} t \\
    &= c^{mk(\beta q-1)}\int_0^{c^{mk} \tau} \fint_{B(z,\tau^{1/m})}
     t^{-\beta q}
    \Bigl( \fint_{(c/2)^{m}t}^{t}
    A_{u_x, c^{-m(k+2)}\delta} f(s,x)^r \hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} s\Bigr)^{q/r}  \hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} x\hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} t \\
    &\lesssim c^{mk(\beta q-1)}\int_0^{\tau} \fint_{B(z,\tau^{1/m})}
    t^{-\beta q}
    \Bigl( 
    {W_r^{(c/2)^m,1,1}} \bigl(A_{u_x, c^{-m(k+3)}\delta} f\bigr)(t,x)\Bigr)^q \hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} x\hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} t, 
\end{align*}
where we used a change of $t$-variable in the second line, and we used $s\geq (c/2)^m t$,   \eqref{eq:martingaleback}  and $c^{-1}\geq 2$ in the third line. The rest of the estimate of $\nrm{H^{\mathrm{ca}}_{\boldsymbol{u}, \delta}f}_{T^{\infty,q,r}_{\beta}}$ follows the case $p<\infty$ in Proposition \ref{prop:modelops-whitneymixed}, and we conclude that, using $\nu = \min\cbrace{q,u_t}$
\begin{align*}
  \|H^{\mathrm{ca}}_{\boldsymbol u,\delta}f\|_{T^{\infty,q,r}_\beta}
  &\lesssim
  \delta^{\gamma}
  \Bigl(\sum_{k=0}^\infty
  c^{\nu mk(\beta+[u_t,q]-\gamma)}
  (1+\ln\delta +mk\ln\tfrac 1c)^{\nu/q}
  \Bigr)^{1/\nu}
  \|f\|_{T^{\infty,q,r}_\beta}\\
    &\le
  \delta^{\gamma}(1+\ln\delta)^{\frac 1q}
  \Bigl(\sum_{k=0}^\infty
  c^{\nu mk(\beta+[u_t,q]-\gamma)}
  (1+mk\ln\tfrac 1c)^{\nu/q}
  \Bigr)^{1/\nu}
  \|f\|_{T^{\infty,q,r}_\beta}\\
      &\lesssim
  \delta^{\gamma}(1+\ln\delta)^{\frac 1q}
  \|f\|_{T^{\infty,q,r}_\beta},
\end{align*}
where we used that $\ln\delta\ge 0$ and
$\beta+[u_t,q]-\gamma> 0$.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
\label{rem:HwODE}
Let $p,q,r \in (0,\infty]$, \(\beta\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}\), \(\delta\in[1,\infty)\). Let
\(\boldsymbol u\in(0,\infty)^2\) satisfy \(u_t,u_x\le r\) and assume that
$$\gamma:=
  \tfrac{n}{m}
  \bigl[\min\cbrace{p,q,u_x},u_x\bigr]<\beta+[u_t,q].
$$
Let $E_t,F_t\subseteq\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}_+$ with $\inf F_t>\sup E_t$.
    Then, for every $\varepsilon>0$, the operator $H^{\mathrm{ca}}_{\boldsymbol u,\delta}$ satisfies the 
    off-diagonal estimate
$$
\|\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_{F_t\times\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^n} H^{\mathrm{ca}}_{\boldsymbol u,\delta} (\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_{E_t\times \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^n}f)\|_{T^{p,q,r}_\beta}
  \lesssim \delta^{\gamma+\varepsilon} 
  \Bigl(\frac{\sup E_t}{\inf F_t}\Bigr)^\eta
  \|f\|_{T^{p,q,r}_\beta}
$$
for some $\eta>0$, and with the $\log$-improvement of $\delta^\epsilon$ when $p=\infty$ as in Proposition~\ref{prop:cabddp>infty}.
This follows upon inspection of the pointwise estimate
\eqref{eq:pointdomHw}. Indeed, since $t>\inf F_t$ and $s<\sup E_t$, only the terms with $c^{mk}\le \sup E_t/\inf F_t$ will contribute. We conclude by summing the geometric series only over these $k$.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:mainestimate}
Let $r \in (1,\infty)$, $\boldsymbol{u} \in [1,\infty)^2$ and $\boldsymbol{v} \in (1,\infty]^2$ be such that
$$\max\cbrace{u_t, u_x} \leq r\leq \min\cbrace{v_t, v_x}.$$ 
Let $\kappa, M\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}$ and suppose that  $T$ is a singular operator of type $(\kappa,m,r,\boldsymbol u,\boldsymbol v, M)$.
Let $p,q\in (0,\infty]$ and $\beta\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}$, and assume the decay condition
\begin{align}
    \tag{d}
    \label{e:main-decay-condition}
    M &> -[u_t,v_t] +\tfrac{n}{m}  {\bigl[\min\cbrace{p,q,u_x},u_x\bigr]} + \tfrac{n}{m}{\bigl[v_x,\max\cbrace{p,q,v_x}\bigr] } + \kappa \\
\intertext{
and the lower and upper bounds
}
    \tag{l}
    \label{e:main-beta-lower-bound}
    \beta &> -[u_t,q]+ \tfrac{n}{m}{\bigl[\min\cbrace{p,q,u_x},u_x\bigr]}, \\
    \tag{u}
    \label{e:main-beta-upper-bound}
    \beta&< \phantom{-}[q,v_t] -\tfrac{n}{m}{\bigl[v_x,\max\cbrace{p,q,v_x}\bigr] }-\kappa.
\end{align}
Then we have for all $f \in L^\infty_c(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+)$,
\begin{equation*}
  \nrm{Tf}_{T^{p,q,r}_{\beta+\kappa}} \lesssim \nrm{f}_{T^{p,q,r}_{\beta}}.
\end{equation*}
If $T$ is causal,  the upper bound \eqref{e:main-beta-upper-bound} is omitted. If $T$ is anti-causal,  the lower bound \eqref{e:main-beta-lower-bound} is omitted.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
We make a few remarks on the assumptions in Theorem \ref{thm:mainestimate}.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
 \item For $u_x\le p,q\le v_x,$ the conditions \eqref{e:main-decay-condition}, \eqref{e:main-beta-lower-bound}, \eqref{e:main-beta-upper-bound} for $\beta$ and $M$  are 
 \[M>-[u_t,v_t]+\kappa,\quad \beta>-[u_t,q], \quad \beta<[q,v_t]-\kappa,\]
 and thus only depend on $u_t,v_t, q$ and $\kappa$. In particular when $p=q=r$,  this yields a sufficient condition for $L^r_\beta(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+)$ boundedness when $\max\cbrace{u_t, u_x} \leq r\leq \min\cbrace{v_t, v_x}.$
\item In the general case, the theorem also provides information about the admissible range of \(p\) and \(q\). Let \(\beta_-\) and \(\beta_+\) denote the lower and upper bounds for \(\beta\), respectively. The decay condition in Theorem~\ref{thm:mainestimate} can then be rewritten as
\[
  M>\beta_- - \beta_+.
\]
Thus, whenever \(\beta_-<\beta_+\), i.e., whenever the admissible range of $\beta$ is non-empty, condition \eqref{e:main-decay-condition} reduces to the negative lower bound
\[
  M>-(\beta_+-\beta_-).
\]
In particular, condition \eqref{e:main-decay-condition} is then automatically satisfied for every $M\geq 0$. Hence, increasing the decay parameter \(M\) beyond \(M=0\) does not enlarge the admissible range of \(p\) and \(q\) in this case.
In contrast, for causal or anti-causal operators, only one of the bounds on \(\beta\) is imposed. The admissible range is then \((\beta_-,\infty)\) or \((-\infty,\beta_+)\), respectively, and is therefore always non-empty. Thus, increasing the decay parameter \(M\) can substantially enlarge the range of \(p\) and \(q\) for which boundedness holds.
\item The proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:mainestimate} can be adapted to $r=1$ and $r=\infty$, but we foresee applications only for $r \in (1,\infty)$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
The conclusion of the theorem is essentially optimal   as can be seen with ``elementary'' examples. Namely,  the various conditions on $M$ and $\beta$ are best possible for the class of singular operators we considered.  Of course, this does not exclude a stronger conclusion for a specific operator.  The upper bound and lower bound on $\beta$ are already optimal for the $L^r_\beta(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+) \to L^r_{\beta+\kappa}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+)$ boundedness of the causal $\kappa$-Hardy operator given 
$$H^+_{\kappa}f(t,x)=\int_0^t (t-s)^{\kappa-1} f(s,x)\hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} s, \qquad (t,x) \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+, $$ and its  anti-causal adjoint $$H^-_{\kappa}f(t,x)=\int_t^\infty  (s-t)^{\kappa-1} f(s,x)\hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} s,  \qquad (t,x) \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+,$$ which are of type $(\kappa, m, r, (1,r),(\infty,r), M)$ for any $m>0, M\in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}$ and $1\le r\le \infty$ when $\kappa>0$. Optimality of the lower bound on $M$  can be checked with spatially lacunary operators of the type \[Tf(t,x)= \sum_{j=1}^N c_j\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_{Q_j}(x) J_\kappa \bigg(s\mapsto \int_{Q_0} \phi(y)f(s,y) \hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} y\bigg)(t),\] where $Q_j$ are unit cubes in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^n$ whose distance to $Q_0$ is $L^j$ for some large $L$,  $J_\kappa$ is the truncated fractional operator given by $$J_\kappa g(t)= \operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_{[1,2]}(t)\int_1^2 (t-s)^{\kappa - 1}g(s) \hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} s, \qquad t \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}_+,$$ and   the positive function $\phi$ and  the positive numbers $c_j$ satisfy  $L^{\rho}$-integrability and $\ell^\sigma$-summability conditions, respecively,  with appropriate $\rho,\sigma$.  The lacunarity implies  that the singular operator bounds do not depend on $N$ and one can compute explicitly the decay $M$.  On the other hand, the appropriate tent space norm of  $Tf$ grows with $N$ for  $f= \operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_{[1,2]\times Q_0}$.  The dependence of $M$ on $\max\{p,q\}$ and $\min\{p,q\}$ is also sharp. We leave the details to the interested readers.
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
As  $r > 1$, we only need to distinguish whether $\min\cbrace{p,q}\ge 1$ or not.
Consider first the case $\min\cbrace{p,q}\ge 1$. 
By Proposition~\ref{prop:tentspacedensityduality}, it suffices to show for $f,g \in L^\infty_c(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+)$ 
that
$$
\int_{{\mathbb R}^{1+n}_+}|Tf||g|  \lesssim \nrm{f}_{\vphantom{T^{p',q',r'}_{-\beta-\kappa}}T^{p,q,r}_\beta} \cdot \nrm{g}_{T^{p',q',r'}_{-\beta-\kappa}}.
$$
To this end, we use the form domination from
Theorem~\ref{thm:maindominationform} and estimate each
of the four terms separately.

For the first term, we note that with $A^{\mathrm{w}}_{r,\kappa}$ as in Lemma \ref{lemma:Whitneymap}, and  using disjointness of the Whitney cubes $\boldsymbol{Q}^{\mathrm{w}}$, $\boldsymbol{Q}^{\mathrm{w}} \subseteq \widetilde{\boldsymbol{Q}}\vphantom{\boldsymbol{Q}}^{\mathrm{w}}$ and Proposition~\ref{prop:tentspacedensityduality},
\begin{align*}
\sum_{Q \in \mathcal{D}} \ell(Q)^{m\kappa} \cdot \ip{f}_{r,\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Q}}\vphantom{\boldsymbol{Q}}^{\mathrm{w}}}\cdot \ip{g}_{\vphantom{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Q}}\vphantom{\boldsymbol{Q}}^{\mathrm{w}}}r',\boldsymbol{Q}^{\mathrm{w}}} \cdot\abs{\boldsymbol{Q}^{\mathrm{w}}} &\lesssim  \int_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+} A^{\mathrm{w}}_{r,\kappa}f(t,x) \cdot A^{\mathrm{w}}_{r',0}g(t,x)\hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} t \hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} x \\
&\le \nrm{A^{\mathrm{w}}_{r,\kappa}f}_{\vphantom{T^{p',q',r'}_{-\beta-\kappa}}T^{p,q,r}_{\beta+\kappa}}\cdot \nrm{A^{\mathrm{w}}_{r',0}g}_{\vphantom{T^{p',q',r'}_{-\beta-\kappa}}T^{p',q',r'}_{-\beta-\kappa}}
\lesssim  \nrm{f}_{\vphantom{T^{p',q',r'}_{-\beta-\kappa}}T^{p,q,r}_\beta} \cdot\nrm{g}_{\vphantom{T^{p',q',r'}_{-\beta-\kappa}}T^{p',q',r'}_{-\beta-\kappa}}.
\end{align*}
Next, for the other terms, we can use Propositions~\ref{prop:modelops-whitneymixed} and~\ref{prop:cabddp>infty} thanks to the conditions on $r$ and $\beta$, noting that  
$(1+\ln\delta)^{1/q}\lesssim \delta^\varepsilon$. 
For the term $(\mathrm{w}$-$\mathrm{w})$, we see that 
\begin{align*}
  \sum_{j=0}^\infty 2^{-jm(M+[u_t,v_t]-\kappa)} &\cdot 
\nrm{H^{\mathrm{w}}_{(r,u_x), 2^{jm}}f}_{\vphantom{T^{p',q',r'}_{-\beta-\kappa}}T^{p,q,r}_\beta}\cdot \nrm{H^{\mathrm{w}}_{(r', v_x'), 2^{jm}}g}_{\vphantom{T^{p',q',r'}_{-\beta-\kappa}}T^{p',q',r'}_{-\beta-\kappa}}
    \\&\lesssim \sum_{j=0}^\infty 2^{-jm\alpha} \cdot\nrm{f}_{\vphantom{T^{p',q',r'}_{-\beta-\kappa}}T^{p,q,r}_\beta} \cdot  \nrm{g}_{\vphantom{T^{p',q',r'}_{-\beta-\kappa}}T^{p',q',r'}_{-\beta-\kappa}},
\end{align*}
where 
\begin{equation}
    \label{eq:alpha}
        \alpha = M +[u_t, v_t]-\kappa -\tfrac{n}{m} {\bigl[\min\cbrace{p,q,u_x},u_x\bigr]} -\tfrac{n}{m}{\bigl[\min\cbrace{p',q',v_x'},v_x'\bigr]}-\varepsilon,
\end{equation}
for any $\varepsilon>0$.
By the decay condition \eqref{e:main-decay-condition}, we can choose $\varepsilon>0$ small enough 
so that $\alpha>0$ and the sum converges. 

The term $(\mathrm{ca}$-$\mathrm{w})$ is estimated similarly to term $(\mathrm{w}$-$\mathrm{w})$, noting that we need $\beta>\gamma-[u_t,q]= \tfrac n m \bigl[\min\cbrace{p,q,u_x},u_x\bigr]-[u_t,q]$
for the estimate of $H^{\mathrm{ca}}_{\boldsymbol{u},2^{jm}}f$, which follows from \eqref{e:main-beta-lower-bound}. This yields  
\begin{align*}
   \sum_{j=0}^\infty 2^{-jm(M+[u_t,v_t]-\kappa)} &\cdot 
\nrm{H^{\mathrm{ca}}_{\boldsymbol{u}, 2^{jm}}f}_{\vphantom{T^{p',q',r'}_{-\beta-\kappa}}T^{p,q,r}_\beta}\cdot \nrm{H^{\mathrm{w}}_{\boldsymbol{v}', 2^{jm}}g}_{\vphantom{T^{p',q',r'}_{-\beta-\kappa}}T^{p',q',r'}_{-\beta-\kappa}}\\
&\lesssim\sum_{j=0}^\infty 2^{-jm\alpha} \cdot\nrm{f}_{\vphantom{T^{p',q',r'}_{-\beta-\kappa}}T^{p,q,r}_\beta} \cdot  \nrm{g}_{T^{p',q',r'}_{-\beta-\kappa}},
\end{align*}
with $\alpha$ as before, so the sum again converges.
Recall that if $T$ is anti-causal, then the term {$(\mathrm{ca}$-$\mathrm{w})$} is not present in the domination from
Theorem~\ref{thm:maindominationform}. Finally, unless $T$ is causal, the term $(\mathrm{w}$-$\mathrm{ca})$ is estimated identically to term $(\mathrm{ca}$-$\mathrm{w})$,
now using \eqref{e:main-beta-upper-bound} for the estimate
of $H^{\mathrm{ca}}_{\boldsymbol{v}', 2^{jm}}g$.

\medskip

Consider now the case $\nu:= {\min\cbrace{p,q}}\in(0,1)$.
{Using Proposition~\ref{prop:tentspacedensityduality}\ref{it:quasiduality}}, it suffices to prove that for $f,g \in L^\infty_c(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+)$
$$
\int_{{\mathbb R}^{1+n}_+}|Tf|^\nu|g|  \lesssim \nrm{f}_{\vphantom{T^{p',q',r'}_{-\beta-\kappa}}T^{p,q,r}_\beta}^\nu \cdot \nrm{g}_{T^{(p/\nu)',(q/\nu)',(r/\nu)'}_{-\nu(\beta+\kappa)}}^{}.
$$
For this we apply Theorem~\ref{thm:quasimaindominationform},
and estimate the four terms similarly to the above arguments.
{For the first term, as before together with  \eqref{eq:rescalenorm} and Proposition~\ref{prop:tentspacedensityduality},  
\begin{align*}
\sum_{Q \in \mathcal{D}} \ell(Q)^{\nu m\kappa} \cdot \ip{f}^\nu_{r,\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Q}}\vphantom{\boldsymbol{Q}}^{\mathrm{w}}}\cdot \ip{g}_{\vphantom{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Q}}\vphantom{\boldsymbol{Q}}^{\mathrm{w}}}({r}/\nu)',\boldsymbol{Q}^{\mathrm{w}}} \cdot\abs{\boldsymbol{Q}^{\mathrm{w}}} & \lesssim \int_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+} \bigl(A^{\mathrm{w}}_{r,\kappa}f(t,x)\bigr)^{\nu} \cdot A^{\mathrm{w}}_{({r}/\nu)',0}g(t,x)\hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} t \hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} x \\
&\le \nrm{A^{\mathrm{w}}_{r,\kappa}f}_{\vphantom{T^{p',q',r'}_{-\beta-\kappa}}T^{p,q,r}_{\beta+\kappa}}^\nu \cdot \nrm{A^{\mathrm{w}}_{({r}/\nu)',0}g}_{T^{(p/\nu)'
   ,(q/\nu)',(r/\nu)'}_{-\nu(\beta+\kappa)}}^{}\\&
\lesssim  \nrm{f}_{\vphantom{T^{p',q',r'}_{-\beta-\kappa}}T^{p,q,r}_\beta}^\nu \cdot\nrm{g}_{T^{(p/\nu)',(q/\nu)',(r/\nu)'}_{-\nu(\beta+\kappa)}}^{}.
\end{align*}}
The last three terms are each estimated by
\begin{align*}
\sum_{j=0}^\infty  2^{-jm\nu(M+[u_t,v_t]-\kappa)} \cdot
&\bigl(2^{jn({\brac{\min\cbrace{p,q,u_x},u_x}}+\varepsilon)} \nrm{f}_{T^{p,q,r}_\beta} \bigr)^\nu\\ &\cdot  2^{jn( {\brac{\min\cbrace{(p/\nu)',(q/\nu)',(v_x/\nu)'},(v_x/\nu)'}}+\varepsilon)} \nrm{g}_{T^{(p/\nu)',(q/\nu)',(r/\nu)'}_{-\nu(\beta+\kappa)}},    
\end{align*}
where assumption \eqref{e:main-decay-condition} shows that the sum converges.
As in the case $\min\cbrace{p,q}\geq 1$, the hypothesis on $\beta$ required for the estimate on $f$ in the term $(\mathrm{ca}$-$\mathrm{w})$
follows from \eqref{e:main-beta-lower-bound}. 
For the estimate on $g$ in term $(\mathrm{w}$-$\mathrm{ca})$, the hypothesis 
$$-\nu(\beta+\kappa)>\tfrac nm{ \bigl[\min\bigl\{(\tfrac{p}{\nu})',(\tfrac{q}{\nu})',(\tfrac{v_x}{\nu})'\bigr\},(\tfrac{v_x}{\nu})'\bigr]}-\bigl[(\tfrac{v_t}{\nu})', (\tfrac q\nu)'\bigr]$$ is needed,
which follows from \eqref{e:main-beta-upper-bound}. 
This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:extension} Let $T$ be a singular operator satisfying the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:mainestimate}and the pointwise almost everywhere Lipschitz estimate
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pointwiseLipschitz}
    |Tf-Tg|\le C \, |T(f-g)|, \qquad f,g \in L^\infty_c(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+)
\end{equation}
for some $C<\infty$.
Then $T$ has a unique bounded extension $\widetilde T:T^{p,q,r}_\beta\to T^{p,q,r}_{\beta+\kappa}$ satisfying for all compact $\boldsymbol{K}\subseteq\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+$, all sequences $(\boldsymbol{K}_j)_j$  of compact sets, with
$\boldsymbol{K}_j\subseteq \text{Int}\, \boldsymbol{K}_{j+1}$,
that exhaust $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+$, and all $f\in T^{p,q,r}_\beta$, that
$$
 \operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_{\boldsymbol{K}} \widetilde Tf:= \lim_{j\to\infty} \operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_{\boldsymbol{K}} T(f\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_{{\boldsymbol{K}}_j}), 
$$
where the limit is in the  norm topology of $T^{p,q,r}_{\beta+\kappa}$.

Moreover, if $T$ is linear, then $\widetilde T$ coincides with the extension by norm continuity if $\max\{p,q\}<\infty$ and by  weak-star continuity if $\min\{p,q\}>1$.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
For linear operators, \eqref{eq:pointwiseLipschitz} always holds with $C=1$. For subadditive operators such that $Tf\ge 0$ and $T(f)=T(-f)$, this also holds with $C=1$.
Indeed, these additional assumptions imply that
$Tf\le Tg+T(f-g)$ and $Tg\le Tf+T(g-f)=Tf+T(f-g)$, hence  \eqref{eq:pointwiseLipschitz}. This covers many subadditive operators such as maximal operators and, more generally,
those coming from a vector-valued linear operator, that is $Tf=\|\mathcal{T}f\|_B$, where $\mathcal{T}$ is linear and $\|\cdot\|_B$ is a norm.
<!-- end remark-11 -->
<!-- remark-12: body_md -->
{This extension in Theorem \ref{thm:extension}  clearly preserves (anti-)causality.}
<!-- end remark-12 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:extension} Let $T$ be as in Theorem \ref{thm:extension}. Then $T$ extends to a unique bounded operator $T^{p,q,r}_{\beta,c}\to T^{p,q,r}_{\beta+\kappa}$, where $T^{p,q,r}_{\beta,c}$ denotes the space of $T^{p,q,r}_\beta$ functions with compact support.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
The pointwise Lipschitz inequality implies $\nrm{Tf-Tg}\lesssim \nrm{T(f-g)}$ for any of the tent space norms above. Hence, $T$   initially defined on $L^\infty_c(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+)$,    can be defined uniquely on the closure of $L^\infty_c(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+)$ in $T^{p,q,r}_\beta$  by continuity  with
$\nrm{Tf}_{T^{p,q,r}_{\beta+\kappa}}\lesssim
  \nrm{f}_{T^{p,q,r}_{\beta}}.$
  If $\max\{p,q\}<\infty$, this closure is all of $T^{p,q,r}_\beta$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:tentspacedensityduality}\ref{it:density}.
  Otherwise, one checks that this closure contains $T^{p,q,r}_{\beta,c}$ (which consists of all compactly supported functions in $L^r(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+)$).
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:annulitobox} Fix $(t_0,x_0) \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+$ and define
\begin{align*}
   \boldsymbol{A}_k&:= (2^{-(k+1)m}t_0, 2^{km}t_0)\times B(x_0,(2^{km}t_0)^{1/m}), &&k \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}},\\
    \boldsymbol{W}&:=(2^{-m}t_0, t_0)\times B(x_0,t_0^{1/m}).
\end{align*}
 Under the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:extension},  
   there exists an $\varepsilon>0$ such that for all $f\in T^{p,q,r}_\beta$ with compact support and  $k\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$ we have
   $$
\nrm{\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_{\boldsymbol{W}}T(f\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+\setminus\boldsymbol{A}_k})}_{T^{p,q,r}_{\beta+\kappa}} \lesssim 2^{-k\varepsilon}\nrm{f\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+\setminus \boldsymbol{A}_k}}_{T^{p,q,r}_{\beta}},
   $$
   where $T$ is the extension from Lemma~\ref{lem:extension}.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Fix  an $f\in T^{p,q,r}_\beta$,  a compact subset $\boldsymbol{K}\subseteq\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+$ and an increasing sequence of compact sets $(\boldsymbol{K}_j)_j$   
that exhaust $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+$. By a finite covering, we may assume that  $\boldsymbol{K} \subseteq \boldsymbol{W}$, and for any $k$ there is an integer $j_k$ such that $\boldsymbol{A}_k\subseteq \boldsymbol{K}_j$ for $j>j_k$, where $\boldsymbol{W}$ and $\boldsymbol{A}_k$ are as in Lemma \ref{lem:annulitobox}. Then $(\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_{\boldsymbol{K}} T(f\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_{\boldsymbol{K}_j}))$ is a Cauchy sequence in $T^{p,q,r}_{\beta+\kappa}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:annulitobox}. Hence, one can set 
$$
  T_{\boldsymbol{K}} f:= \lim_{j\to\infty} \operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_{\boldsymbol{K}} T(f\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_{\boldsymbol{K}_j} ).
$$
Observe that for fixed $\boldsymbol{K}$,  the limit does not  depend on the choice of the exhausting sequence. 
Moreover, 
$\nrm{T_{\boldsymbol{K}}f}_{T^{p,q,r}_{\beta+\kappa}}\lesssim \nrm{f}_{T^{p,q,r}_{\beta}}$ 
with implicit constant independent of $f$ and ${\boldsymbol{K}}$. 
Clearly, $T_{\boldsymbol{K}}f$ and $T_{\tilde {\boldsymbol{K}}}f$ agree on the intersection of two compact sets ${\boldsymbol{K}}, \tilde {\boldsymbol{K}}$. Thus we may define $\widetilde Tf$ by
$\widetilde Tf(t,x):= T_{\boldsymbol{K}}f(t,x)$ if $(t,x)\in {\boldsymbol{K}}$. By monotone convergence  we have 
\begin{equation*} 
    \nrm{\widetilde Tf}_{T^{p,q,r}_{\beta+\kappa}}\eqsim
  \sup_{\boldsymbol{K}} \,\nrm{ T_{\boldsymbol{K}} f}_{T^{p,q,r}_{\beta+\kappa}},    
\end{equation*}
so this yields a well-defined and bounded extension 
$ \widetilde T:T^{p,q,r}_\beta\to T^{p,q,r}_{\beta+\kappa}$ of $T$.

Uniqueness is immediate. Moreover, it is easy to see that when  $T$ is  linear, this extension  coincides with the extension by 
strong density if $\max\{p,q\}<\infty$ and weak-star density 
if $\min\{p,q\}>1$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:tentspacedensityduality}\ref{it:density}.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
By assumption, we know that $f$ has compact support and $f\in L^r(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+)$. Fix $k \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$ and define $f_k:=f\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+\setminus \boldsymbol{A}_k}$. 
We will first consider the case $\min\cbrace{p,q}\ge 1$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:tentspacedensityduality}\ref{it:duality}, it suffices to control $
\int_{\boldsymbol{W}}\abs{Tf_k}\abs{g} $ for bounded $g$ with support in $\boldsymbol{W}$, where $T$ is the extension from Lemma~\ref{lem:extension}. We note that this extension satisfies Definition~\ref{def:ODE}, extended  to functions in $L^r(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+)$ with compact support by density.  One can thus perform the estimates on this integral leading to Theorem~\ref{thm:maindominationform}, i.e.,
    \begin{align*}
\int_{\boldsymbol{W}}&\abs{Tf_k}\abs{g} 
\lesssim 
\sum_{Q \in \mathcal{D}} \ell(Q)^{m\kappa} \cdot \ip{f_k}_{r,\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Q}}\vphantom{\boldsymbol{Q}}^{\mathrm{w}}}\cdot \ip{g}_{\vphantom{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Q}}\vphantom{\boldsymbol{Q}}^{\mathrm{w}}}r',\boldsymbol{Q}^{\mathrm{w}}} \cdot\abs{\boldsymbol{Q}^{\mathrm{w}}}
&& \\
&+\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} 2^{-jm\br{M+[u_t,v_t]-\kappa}} \cdot \int_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+}t^\kappa\cdot   H^{\mathrm{w}}_{(r,u_x),2^{jm}}f_k(t,x)\cdot H^{\mathrm{w}}_{(r',v_x'), 2^{jm}}g(t,x)\hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} x\hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} t  &&
\text{$(\mathrm{w}$-$\mathrm{w})$}\\
&+\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} 2^{-jm\br{M+[u_t,v_t]-\kappa}} \cdot \int_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+}t^\kappa\cdot   H^{\mathrm{ca}}_{\boldsymbol{u},2^{jm}}f_k(t,x)\cdot H^{\mathrm{w}}_{\boldsymbol{v}', 2^{jm}}g(t,x)\hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} x\hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} t &&\text{$(\mathrm{ca}$-$\mathrm{w})$}\\
&+\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} 2^{-jm\br{M+[u_t,v_t]-\kappa}} \cdot
\int_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+}t^\kappa\cdot   H^{\mathrm{w}}_{\boldsymbol{u},2^{jm}}f_k(t,x)\cdot H^{\mathrm{ca}}_{\boldsymbol{v}', 2^{jm}}g(t,x)\hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} x\hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} t. &&\text{$(\mathrm{w}$-$\mathrm{ca})$}.
\end{align*}
 The idea is to leverage the distance between the supports of $f_k$ and $g$.
 

Clearly, for $k$ larger than some number depending only on dimension, $\ip{f_k}_{r,\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Q}}\vphantom{\boldsymbol{Q}}^{\mathrm{w}}}\cdot \ip{g}_{\vphantom{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Q}}\vphantom{\boldsymbol{Q}}^{\mathrm{w}}}r',\boldsymbol{Q}^{\mathrm{w}}}=0$ for all $Q\in \mathcal{D}$, so the first term vanishes and it remains to control the three other terms. To simplify the exposition, we assume that the constant $c$ in the definition of the operator  $H^{\mathrm{w}}$   is $\tfrac12$. The general case can be obtained using a finite covering in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}_+$. 

For the (w-w) term, we observe that from the support condition on $g$, we only have $H^\mathrm{w} g(t,x) \neq 0$ if $t\in (2^{-m}t_0,{2^m} t_0)$ and $|x-x_0|\le 2^jt^{1/m}+{t_0}^{1/m}$. 
Furthermore, by the support of $f_k$ we only have $H^\mathrm{w} f_k(t,x) \neq 0$ if $|x-x_0|\ge 2^k t_0^{1/m}- 2^j t^{1/m}$. Hence the {integrand} vanishes unless {
$2^k t_0^{1/m} \le  2^{j+1} t^{1/m}+t_0^{1/m} < (2^{j+2}+1) t_0^{1/m}$ and thus $j+2\ge k$.} Therefore, the series in the (w-w)-term starts at {$j=k-2$} and we get the decay $2^{-k m\alpha}$ from the argument in 
Theorem~\ref{thm:maindominationform} using \eqref{e:main-decay-condition} with  $\alpha$  given by \eqref{eq:alpha}, i.e., we can use $\varepsilon := m\alpha$ for the (w-w)-term. 

For the (ca-w) term, as before  we only have $H^\mathrm{w} g(t,x) \neq 0$ if $t\in (2^{-m}t_0,{2^m} t_0)$ and $|x-x_0|\le 2^jt^{1/m}+{t_0}^{1/m}$.
 If {$j\le k-3$}, the only contributions of $f_k$ come from its values near the boundary. 
We apply the off-diagonal estimates for $H^{\mathrm{ca}}_{\boldsymbol{u},2^{jm}}$ 
 noted in Remark~\ref{rem:HwODE} with $E_t=(0,2^{-(k+1)m}t_0)$
 and $F_t= (2^{-m}t_0,\infty)$, which shows that the series for  {$j\leq k-3$} in the (ca-w) term is bounded by 
\[   {\sum_{j=0}^{k-3} 2^{-jm\alpha}\cdot 2^{-km\eta} }\cdot\nrm{f_k}_{\vphantom{T^{p',q',r'}_{-\beta-\kappa}}T^{p,q,r}_\beta} \cdot  \nrm{g}_{\vphantom{T^{p',q',r'}_{-\beta-\kappa}}T^{p',q',r'}_{-\beta-\kappa}} \lesssim  2^{-km\eta} \cdot\nrm{f_k}_{\vphantom{T^{p',q',r'}_{-\beta-\kappa}}T^{p,q,r}_\beta} \cdot  \nrm{g}_{\vphantom{T^{p',q',r'}_{-\beta-\kappa}}T^{p',q',r'}_{-\beta-\kappa}},\]
for some $\eta>0$.
 The series for {$j\geq k-2$} is controlled by $2^{-k m\alpha} \cdot\nrm{f_k}_{\vphantom{T^{p',q',r'}_{-\beta-\kappa}}T^{p,q,r}_\beta} \cdot  \nrm{g}_{\vphantom{T^{p',q',r'}_{-\beta-\kappa}}T^{p',q',r'}_{-\beta-\kappa}}$ as for the (w-w)-term. Hence, for the  (ca-w)-term we can use $\varepsilon := m\min\cbrace{\alpha,\eta}$.

Finally, the (w-ca) term is handled differently. Fix $j$ and split the integral in the (w-ca) series according to $t\in (2^{(-1+\ell)m}t_0,2^{\ell m}t_0)$ for $\ell\ge 0$. Considering the $x$-supports of $f_k$ and $g$ shows that the integrand vanishes unless {$j+\ell+1\ge k$}.
We apply the off-diagonal estimates for $H^{\mathrm{ca}}_{\boldsymbol{v}',2^{jm}}$ 
 noted in Remark~\ref{rem:HwODE} with $E_t=(0,t_0)$
 and $F_t= (2^{(\ell-1)m}t_0,\infty)$.
 By these bounds for the $H^\mathrm{ca}$ and $H^\mathrm{w}$ operators, the (w-ca) term is  
\[\lesssim \sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\sum_{\ell=0}^\infty  {\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_{j+\ell+1\ge k}} \cdot \, 2^{-jm\alpha}\cdot  2^{-\ell m\eta} \cdot\nrm{f_k}_{\vphantom{T^{p',q',r'}_{-\beta-\kappa}}T^{p,q,r}_\beta} \cdot  \nrm{g}_{\vphantom{T^{p',q',r'}_{-\beta-\kappa}}T^{p',q',r'}_{-\beta-\kappa}},\]
for some $\eta>0$, which is controlled by 
\[   2^{-k \varepsilon } \cdot\nrm{f_k}_{\vphantom{T^{p',q',r'}_{-\beta-\kappa}}T^{p,q,r}_\beta} \cdot  \nrm{g}_{\vphantom{T^{p',q',r'}_{-\beta-\kappa}}T^{p',q',r'}_{-\beta-\kappa}}\]
for  $\varepsilon <m \min\{\alpha,\eta\}$.
This finishes the proof in the case $\min\{p,q\}\geq 1$.
The proof for $\min\{p,q\}<1$ is similar, using instead Theorem~\ref{thm:quasimaindominationform} applied to the extension.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- remark-13: body_md -->
It is possible to do a purely dyadic version of Lemma~\ref{lem:annulitobox} based on the decomposition in Proposition~\ref{prop:decomposition}
or the decomposition~\eqref{eq:pdecomp} by taking $g$ supported in a Whitney cube $\boldsymbol{P}^{\mathrm{w}}$ and $f_k$ supported in the complement of the union of all Whitney regions $\boldsymbol{Q}^{\mathrm{w}}$ with $2^{-km}\ell(P)\le \ell(Q)\le 2^{km}\ell(P)$ with $d(Q,P)\le 2^k\ell(P)$. This indicates that 
we did not lose too much information in controlling these decompositions using the model operators.
<!-- end remark-13 -->
<!-- remark-14: body_md -->
The space $L^\infty_c(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+)$ has the advantage of being contained in all tent spaces.  Yet, it could happen that a singular operator is defined on a larger space to start with and other density procedures are available, leading to the same extension. For example,  the space of functions of bounded support (not necessarily away from the boundary) in $L^r(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+; t^{-\beta r}\hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} t\hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} x)\cap T^{p,\infty,r}_\beta$ is dense in $T^{p,\infty,r}_\beta$ for $p\in (0,\infty)$, $r\in (1,\infty)$ and  $\beta\in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}$. This was proved in \cite[Lemma 5.2]{HR23} when $\beta=0$ and the proof also holds for $0<p\le 1$. If the singular operator $T$ is initially defined on that dense space, one can check that our decompositions and estimates go through also for 
functions of bounded support, showing that, under the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:mainestimate}, 
$T$ extends uniquely from this dense subspace to $T^{p,\infty,r}_\beta$.
The key point is that bounded support allows us to start the decomposition in 
Proposition~\ref{prop:decomposition} from a top Carleson box $\boldsymbol{Q}^{\mathrm{ca}}_0$.
It does not seem that  we have density of some space of functions with bounded support when $p=\infty$ and our extension is the only one we know.
<!-- end remark-14 -->
<!-- cor-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:q=r=2} Let $T$ be a  singular operator of type $(\kappa, m, 2, (1,u_x), (\infty,v_x), M)$ with $\kappa, M\in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}$ and $u_x,v_x\in [1,\infty]$. Let $p\in (0,\infty]$ and $\beta\in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}$. Then     $T$ extends to a bounded operator from $T^{p,2,2}_{\beta}$ to $T^{p,2,2}_{\beta+\kappa}$ if $T$ satisfies the pointwise Lipschitz property and one of the following holds
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
    \item \label{it:causalpge2} $T$ is causal, $u_x=2, v_x\ge 2$, $p\ge 2$ and   
    \begin{align*}
    \beta&>-\tfrac 12 
    \\
    M_{\textup{AH}}& > \tfrac{n}{m} \cdot  [2,\max \{p,v_x\}].
    \end{align*}
    \item \label{it:anticausalpge2} $T$ is anti-causal, $u_x=2, v_x\ge 2$, $p\ge 2$ and  \begin{align*}
    \beta&<\tfrac 12 - \tfrac{n}{m} \cdot [v_x,\max\cbrace{p,v_x}]-\kappa    \\M_{\textup{AH}} &> \tfrac{n}{m} \cdot  [2,\max \{p,v_x\}].
    \end{align*}
    \item \label{it:causalple2} $T$ is causal, $u_x\le 2, v_x= 2$, $p\le 2$ and  \begin{align*}
    \beta&>-\tfrac 12 +\tfrac{n}{m} \cdot  [ \min\cbrace{p,u_x},u_x]\\ M_{\textup{AH}} &> \tfrac{n}{m} \cdot  [\min \{p,u_x\}, 2].\end{align*}
     \item \label{it:anticausalple2} $T$ is anti-causal, $u_x\le 2, v_x= 2$, $p\le 2$ and
     \begin{align*}
     \beta&<\tfrac 12 -\kappa \\M_{\textup{AH}}& > \tfrac{n}{m} \cdot  [\min \{p,u_x\}, 2].
     \end{align*}
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end cor-1 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
These are simple verifications from Theorem~\ref{thm:mainestimate}. The lower bound on $M_{\text{AH}}$ follows from \eqref{e:main-decay-condition}, the lower bound on $\beta$ if $T$ is causal from \eqref{e:main-beta-lower-bound}, and the upper bound on $\beta$ if $T$ is anti-causal from \eqref{e:main-beta-upper-bound}.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- remark-15: body_md -->
\label{rem:L2bdd}
    Note that lower bounds for $M_{\text{AH}}$ are $p$-dependent.
    An interesting  particular case  is $p=u_x=v_x=2$ which arises in each item: the condition  $M_{\text{AH}}>0$ yields   $L^2_{\beta}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+)$ to $L^2_{\beta+\kappa}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+)$ boundedness for \textbf{all} $\beta$ in the given range, whereas we  are only assuming  localized $L^2$-boundedness on Whitney regions.  Thus, if one knows only such boundedness for one value of $\beta$, as is often the case, then boundedness for any $\beta$ as above follows. 
    For maximal regularity operators this is a well-known phenomenon, see, e.g., \cite{CK18}.
<!-- end remark-15 -->
<!-- remark-16: body_md -->
\cite[Corollary~2 and Corollary 3]{AH25a} also establish $T^{\infty,2, 2}_{\beta,[p,1]} \to T^{\infty,2,2}_{\beta+\kappa,[p,1]}$ boundedness for the adjoint $T^*$  in the range  $0<p<1$ and with $\beta$ for which one has $T^{p,2,2}_{-\beta-\kappa}$ to $T^{p,2,2}_{-\beta}$ boundedness for the singular integral operator $T$. This is obtained using duality since $T^{\infty,2, 2}_{\beta,[p,1]}$ (which we do not define here) is identified with the dual space of $T^{p,2, 2}_{-\beta}$ in the duality of $L^2(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+, \hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} t\hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} x)$. We can also  recover this result differently with the following argument.  Indeed, $T^*$  is easily seen to be a singular operator to which the form domination applies.   Applying the required model operator boundedness, see Lemma~\ref{lemma:Whitneymap} and Proposition \ref{prop:cabddp>infty}, and Theorem~\ref{thm:mainestimate} proves  $T^{\infty,\infty,2}_{\beta+ \frac nm [p,1]}$ to $T^{\infty,\infty,2}_{\beta+ \frac nm [p,1]+\kappa}$ boundedness of $T^*$ under appropriate conditions on $\beta+ \frac nm [p,1]$ and $M_{\text{AH}}$. As \cite[Proposition 3.27]{Haa26}, re-expressed in our context, shows that $T^{\infty,2,2}_{\beta,[p,1]} = T^{\infty,\infty,2}_{\beta+ \frac nm [p,1]}$ isomorphically, we conclude using these isomorphisms. As before, one can check that we get the same conditions on $\beta, p$ with a smaller lower bound on the decay parameter.
<!-- end remark-16 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:cz}
Let $r\in(1,\infty)$, $p,q\in(0,\infty]$ and $\beta\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}$, and assume that
$$
  \gamma:= 1-n\cdot \bigl[\min\cbrace{p,q,1},1\bigr]>0,
$$
or equivalently, $p,q>\frac{n}{n+1}$.
\begin{itemize}
    \item 
    If $S:L^r(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+)\to L^r(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+)$ is bounded and has a CZ kernel $k$
with pointwise upper bounds \eqref{eq:kest},
then $S: T^{p,q,r}_\beta\to T^{p,q,r}_\beta$ is bounded
if $q^{-1}-\gamma<\beta <q^{-1}$.
\item 
If $S^+:L^r(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+)\to L^r(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+)$ is bounded and has a causal 
CZ kernel $k^+$ as in \eqref{eq:kplus} with pointwise upper bounds \eqref{eq:kest}
on $k$,
then $S^+: T^{p,q,r}_\beta\to T^{p,q,r}_\beta$ is bounded
if $q^{-1}-\gamma<\beta$.
\item 
If $S^-:L^r(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+)\to L^r(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+)$ is bounded and has an anti-causal 
CZ kernel $k^-$ as in \eqref{eq:kminus} with pointwise upper bounds \eqref{eq:kest}
on $k$,
then $S^-: T^{p,q,r}_\beta\to T^{p,q,r}_\beta$ is bounded
if $\beta<q^{-1}$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- remark-17: body_md -->
~
\begin{itemize}
    \item Note that in the Banach range $1\le p,q\le \infty$, we have $\gamma=1$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:cz}.
In particular this recovers \cite[Theorem 5.1]{HR23}.
Indeed, for $S^+$ this uses $1<p<\infty$, $q=\infty$ and $\beta=0$, for which the above hypothesis holds. 
For $S^-$ this uses $1<p<\infty$, $q=1$ and $\beta=0$, for which the above hypothesis also holds using an equivalent  norm on $T^{p,1,r}_0$ based on a Carleson functional \cite[Theorem 3]{CMS85}.
Our Theorem~\ref{thm:cz} also answers the open problem posed in the second bullet in 
\cite[Section 6.1]{HR23}, in that it gives boundedness results for Calder\'on--Zygmund operators on general tent spaces.
\item  It is interesting to note that our strategy to obtain tent space estimates is completely different from that in \cite{HR23}. We exclusively rely on the pointwise upper bound \eqref{eq:kest}, yet we assume $L^r(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+)$-boundedness, which usually uses some regularity on $k$. In \cite{HR23}, H\"older regularity of $k$ is used  to show  weak $L^1(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+)$-boundedness of the SIO and the Lerner maximally truncated SIO,
\cite[Lemma 3.1 and Proposition 3.2]{HR23}, which in turn is used in the proof of
$L^r(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+)$ boundedness of $S, S^+$ and $S^-$ for $1<r<\infty$. The size estimate \eqref{eq:kest} was also needed in \cite{HR23} to show the weak $L^1(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+)$-estimates and to bound the 
technical $x$-separation term $II_1$ in the proof of the sparse domination (Theorem 4.1). 
\end{itemize}
<!-- end remark-17 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:DBresODEs}
    Let $p_-(DB)<p_1<p_2<p_+(DB)$ and define the bisector
    $$
S_\mu:=\bigl\{t\in \ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}: |\Im (t)| \le \tan(\mu) |\Re (t)| \bigr\}
    $$
with $0<\mu<\frac{\pi}{2}$ depending on $B$.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
    \item \label{it:DBODE1}
    If $[p_1,p_2]\le \frac1n$, then the estimate 
\begin{equation*}   
\nrm{(I+it DB)^{-1} f}_{L^{p_2}}
\lesssim |t|^{-n[p_1,p_2]}\nrm{f}_{L^{p_1}}    
\end{equation*}
holds for all $0\ne t\in S_\mu$ and all $f\in \overline{R(D)}$.
    \item \label{it:DBODE2}
    If $[p_1,p_2]< \frac1n$, there exists
$c>0$ such that 
the off-diagonal estimates  
\begin{equation*}  
\nrm{\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_F tDB(I+t^2 (DB)^2)^{-1} (f\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_E) }_{L^{p_2}}
\lesssim |t|^{-n[p_1,p_2]}
 e^{-c \frac{d(E,F)}{|t|}}
\nrm{f\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_E}_{L^{p_1}}    
\end{equation*}
hold for all $0\ne t\in S_\mu$, all $E,F\subseteq \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^n$, and all $f\in L^{p_1}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^n; \ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}^{1+n})$.
\item \label{item:ODEsN}
If $[p_1,p_2]< \frac{N}{n}$ for some $N\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$, then
there exists
$c>0$ and $0\leq \theta<1$ such that
the off-diagonal estimates
\begin{equation*} 
\nrm{\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_F (I+it DB)^{-1} (f\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_E) }_{L^{p_2}}
\lesssim |t|^{-n[p_1,p_2]}
\Bigl(\frac {|t|}{d(E,F)}\Bigr)^{(2N-1)\theta}  e^{-c \frac{d(E,F)}{|t|}}
\nrm{f\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_E}_{L^{p_1}}    
\end{equation*}
hold for all $0\ne t\in S_\mu$, all $E,F\subseteq \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^n$
with $d(E,F)>0$, and all $f\in L^{p_1}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^n; \ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}^{1+n})$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
For \ref{it:DBODE1} we use the Sobolev embedding $ W^{1,p_1} \subseteq L^{p_2}$ and the ellipticity estimate
  $\nrm{\nabla u}_{L^p}\lesssim \nrm{Du}_{L^p}$ for $u\in \overline{R(D)}$, which follows from Riesz transform bounds for $p \in (1,\infty)$.
  Details are in \cite[Section 15.3, Claim 18]{AS16}.

For \ref{it:DBODE2} we first claim the estimate
$$
\nrm{tDB(I+t^2 (DB)^2)^{-1} f }_{L^{p_2}}
\lesssim |t|^{-n[p_1,p_2]}
\nrm{f}_{L^{p_1}}.  
$$
For $f\in \overline{R(DB)} = \overline{R(D)}$,
 this follows from \ref{it:DBODE1} upon writing
$$
  tDB(I+t^2 (DB)^2)^{-1}=
  \tfrac 1{2i}\bigl((I-itDB)^{-1}-(I+itDB)^{-1}\bigr).
$$
For $f\in N(DB)$, we have $tDB(I+t^2 (DB)^2)^{-1} f =0$. Thus, \eqref{eq:hodge} proves the claim for general $f\in L^{p_1}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^n; \ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}^{1+n})$.

The off-diagonal estimate in \ref{it:DBODE2} for the operator
$Q:=\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_F tDB(I+t^2 (DB)^2)^{-1}\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_E$ 
follows by interpolation.
Indeed, taking $0<\theta<1$
    sufficiently close to $1$ and defining $\tilde p_1,\tilde p_2$ by the relations  $[p_1,2]=\theta[\tilde p_1,2]$
and $[2,p_2]=\theta[2,\tilde p_2]$, we have 
$p_-(DB)<\tilde p_1<\tilde p_2<p_+(DB)$ and 
    $[\tilde p_1,\tilde p_2]\le \frac1n$.
By the above claim,
$$
  \nrm{Q}_{L^{\tilde p_1}(E)\to 
L^{\tilde p_2}(F)}\lesssim |t|^{-n[\tilde p_1,\tilde p_2]}.
$$
Exponential $L^2$ off-diagonal estimates 
$$
  \nrm{Q}_{L^2(E)\to 
L^2(F)}\lesssim e^{-c d(E,F)/|t|}
$$
for $DB$ are proved as in \cite[Lemma 5.3]{CMcM13}.
Interpolation now gives \ref{it:DBODE2} upon replacing $c(1-\theta)$ by $c$ and noting that
$\theta[\tilde p_1, \tilde p_2]= [p_1,p_2]$.

For \ref{item:ODEsN}, start by assuming $[p_1,p_2]\le \frac1n$.
The argument for \ref{it:DBODE2}  does not directly apply to the resolvents 
$(I+it DB)^{-1}$, since the estimate
\ref{it:DBODE1} only holds for $f\in \overline{R(D)}$.
The non-trivial observation is that it is nevertheless possible to obtain an 
$L^{p_1}(E)\to L^{p_2}(F)$ estimate for all
$f\in L^{p_1}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^n; \ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}^{1+n})$ if $d(E,F)>0$.
To see this, we consider the commutator with a Lipschitz function $\eta:\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^n\to \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}$, such that $\eta=1$ on $F$, $\eta=0$ on $E$, and $\nrm{\nabla\eta}_\infty\lesssim 1/d(E,F)$.
Note the commutator identity
\begin{align} \label{eq:firstcomm} \begin{aligned}
     \operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_F(I+itDB)^{-1}\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_E&= \operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_F[\eta, (I+itDB)^{-1}]\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_E \\
 &= -\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_F(I+itDB)^{-1} it[\eta, D]B(I+itDB)^{-1}\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_E 
\end{aligned}\end{align}
and that $[\eta,D]$ is a multiplier by a matrix
pointwise bounded by $|\nabla\eta|$.
We can further choose $\eta$ so that 
$G:= \operatorname{supp}{\nabla\eta}$ satisfies
$d(F,G)\eqsim d(G,E)\eqsim d(E,F)$.

Given $f\in L^{p_1}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^n; \ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}^{1+n})$, we write $\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_E f=f_1+f_0$ using \eqref{eq:hodge}, with $f_1\in\overline{R(DB)}$
and $f_0\in N(DB)$.
For $f_1$ we estimate
$$
\Bigl\|\Bigl(\frac 1{I+itDB} t[\eta, D]B\Bigr) \Bigl( \frac 1{I+itDB} \Bigr)f_1\Bigr\|_{L^{p_2}}\lesssim
\frac {|t|}{d(E,F)} |t|^{-n[p_1,p_2]} \nrm{f_1}_{L^{p_1}},
$$
using $L^{p_2}$-boundedness of the operator in the left parenthesis, and \ref{it:DBODE1} for the right one.
For $f_0$ we estimate
\begin{align*}
\Bigl\|\Bigl(\frac 1{I+itDB}\Bigr) \Bigl( t[\eta, D]B 
\frac 1{I+itDB} \Bigr)f_0\Bigr\|_{L^{p_2}}
&\lesssim |t|^{-n[p_1,p_2]} \nrm{ t[\eta, D]B f_0}_{L^{p_1}}\\
&\lesssim
|t|^{-n[p_1,p_2]}\frac {|t|}{d(E,F)}  \nrm{f_0}_{L^{p_1}}, 
\end{align*}
using that $(I+itDB)^{-1}f_0= f_0\in N(DB)$ and
that $[\eta,D]B f_0= -D(\eta Bf_0)\in \overline{R(D)}$, i.e.,  \ref{it:DBODE1} applies 
to the operator in the left parenthesis.
Using \eqref{eq:hodge}, we have shown that 
\begin{equation}  \label{eq:resOD}
\nrm{\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_F (I+it DB)^{-1} (f\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_E) }_{L^{p_2}}
\lesssim |t|^{-n[p_1,p_2]}
\frac {|t|}{d(E,F)}
\nrm{f\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_E}_{L^{p_1}}.     
\end{equation}

In general, if $[p_1,p_2]<\frac{ N}{n}$, we can iterate 
the argument with the commutator \eqref{eq:firstcomm}.
To this end, consider a chain of exponents
$$
  p_1= q_0<q_1<q_2<\ldots < q_N= p_2,
$$
where $n[q_{j-1},q_j]\le 1$ for $j=1,2,\ldots, N$.
Here \eqref{eq:resOD} applies with $p_1,p_2$ replaced
by $q_{j-1}, q_j$, and iterated use of 
\eqref{eq:firstcomm} proves that 
$$
\nrm{\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_F (I+it DB)^{-1} (f\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_E) }_{L^{p_2}}
\lesssim |t|^{-n[p_1,p_2]}
\Bigl(\frac {|t|}{d(E,F)}\Bigr)^{2N-1}
\nrm{f\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_E}_{L^{p_1}}.  
$$
Interpolation with the exponential $L^2$ off-diagonal estimates as in \ref{it:DBODE2} now proves 
the off-diagonal estimates \ref{item:ODEsN}, which completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- remark-18: body_md -->
To appreciate the off-diagonal estimates in Lemma \ref{lem:DBresODEs}\ref{item:ODEsN},
it is instructive to consider the case $B=I$.
Using the identity
$$
  (I-t^2 \delta d)(I-t^2 d\delta)= I-t^2 \Delta, 
$$
where $d$ and $\delta$ are the exterior and interior derivatives on vector fields, the formula
$$
\frac 1{I+itD}= 
\begin{bmatrix}
    1 & it\operatorname{div} \\ -it\nabla & I-t^2\delta d
\end{bmatrix}
\frac 1{I-t^2 \Delta}
$$
follows. 
This reveals that the $(2,2)$-component of the 
matrix kernel of $(I+itD)^{-1}$ contains terms with
second derivatives of Bessel potentials.
This yields a Calder\'on--Zygmund kernel near the diagonal, but a smooth exponentially decaying kernel
away from the diagonal.
In particular we see that the estimate \ref{it:DBODE2} is not possible for the resolvents.
<!-- end remark-18 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:beurling}
Consider a perturbed Dirac operator $DB$, where we write $B$ for the matrix multiplier on $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^n$.
  Let $p_\pm:= p_\pm(DB)$,  $r \in (p_-,p_+)$, and $\beta\in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}$. Suppose that $p,q\in(0,\infty]$ satisfy
$$
n\bigl[\min\cbrace{p,q,p_-},p_-\bigr] +
    n\bigl[p_+,\max\cbrace{p,q,p_+}\bigr] < 1.
$$
  Then $S^+$ is bounded on  $T^{p,q,r}_{\beta}$ $($of $\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}^{1+n}$-valued functions$)$ 
  if 
\begin{gather*}
    \beta>\tfrac{1}{q}-1+n\bigl[\min\cbrace{p,q,p_-},p_-\bigr].
\end{gather*}
$S^-$ is bounded on  $T^{p,q,r}_{\beta}$ $($of $\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}^{1+n}$-valued functions$)$ if
\begin{gather*}
 \beta< \tfrac 1q-n\bigl[p_+,\max\cbrace{p,q,p_+}\bigr] 
\end{gather*}

The maximal regularity operators $T^\pm$ for the Poisson semigroup are bounded on  $T^{p,q,r}_{\beta}$ 
under the same conditions as for $S^\pm$, but with 
$p_\pm:=p_\pm(L)$.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- remark-19: body_md -->
The $T^{p,2,2}_{1/2}$ boundedness of $T^+$ was shown in
  \cite[Proposition~1.7]{AKMP12}. Recall that
  $\min\cbrace{[p_-(L),2], [2,p_+(L)]}> \frac1n$ if $n\ge 3$, while $p_-(L)=1$ and $p_+(L)=\infty$ if $n=1,2$.
  Setting $q=r=2$ and
  $\beta=1/2$,  Theorem~\ref{thm:beurling} 
  recovers this result 
  in dimension $1\le n\le 4$, while 
  for $n\ge 5$, we obtain here 
  $$
    \frac{2n}{n+4}-\varepsilon<p<\frac{2n}{n-4}+\varepsilon',
  $$
  with $\varepsilon,\varepsilon'>0$ depending on $L$, which is a strict improvement. When $A$ has real coefficients, the range for $p$ is $(\tfrac{n}{n+1},\infty]$,  since $p_-(L)=1$ and $p_+(L)=\infty$ in all dimensions.
<!-- end remark-19 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Consider first $T^+$ and let $p_-(L)<p_1<r<p_2<p_+(L)$. By
    Proposition~\ref{prop:compareAH} and Theorem~\ref{thm:mainestimate}, it suffices to show that $T^+$ is a singular integral operator of type $(0,1,r,p_1,p_2,0)$ in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:kernelODE},
    since $p_1>p_-(L)$ and $p_2<p_+(L)$ are arbitrary.
    Using the symbol $\psi(\lambda)= \lambda e^{-\lambda}1_{\Re(\lambda)>0}$, the operator-valued kernel of $T^+$ is
    $$
      K(t,s)=\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_{s<t}\ (t-s)^{-1} \psi((t-s)\sqrt{L}).
    $$ 
    The boundedness of $T^+$ on $L^r(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+)$ follows from  
    $L^r$-maximal regularity of $\sqrt{L}$ on $L^r(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{n})$, which is a consequence of the 
     $H^\infty$-functional calculus on the same space, see \cite{KW04}.
    Off-diagonal estimates 
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:maxregdecay}
      \nrm{\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_F \psi(\tau\sqrt{L})(f \operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_E )}_{L^{p_2}}\lesssim 
      \tau^{-n[p_1,p_2]}(1+d(E,F)/\tau)^{-1-n[p_1,p_2]}
      \nrm{f\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_E }_{L^{p_1}}        
    \end{equation}
    follow from
    \cite[Proposition 12.7]{Auscher-Egert2023-book}, where again, we drop the $x$-subscript in the notation.
    We note that this is stated only for $p_2=2$,
    but inspecting the proof reveals that it goes through for any $p_2<p_+(L)$.
    This proves the result for $T^+$, and the proof for $T^-$ is similar.
    
    Consider next $S^+$, where we now let
     $p_-(DB)<p_1<r<p_2<p_+(DB)$.
    Once the off-diagonal estimates \eqref{eq:maxregdecay}, with $\sqrt{L}$ replaced
    by $DB$, for the operator-valued kernel
    $$
      K(t,s)=\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_{s<t}\ (t-s)^{-1} \psi((t-s)DB)
    $$ 
    have been proved, the proof for $S^\pm$ is analogous to the proof for $T^\pm$. 
    These off-diagonal estimates however are more 
    complicated to see due to the non-injectivity
    of $DB$ and, with this optimal order of decay, are not in the literature.
    To this end, let $\alpha>0$ and consider the auxiliary symbol
    $\psi_\alpha(\lambda)= \lambda^\alpha e^{-\lambda}1_{\Re(\lambda)>0}$.
    By Dunford--Riesz calculus
    \begin{equation}   \label{eq:dunford}
      \psi_\alpha(\tau DB)= \frac 1{2\pi i}
      \int_{\gamma} \frac{(\tau \lambda)^\alpha e^{-\tau\lambda}}{I-\lambda^{-1}DB} \frac{d\lambda}\lambda, 
    \end{equation}
    where $\tau>0$ and $\gamma:=\partial S_{\nu+}$ with
    $S_{\nu+}:= \{\lambda \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}:|\arg\lambda\, |<\nu\}$ for $\pi/2-\mu<\nu<\pi/2$ with $\mu$ as in Lemma~\ref{lem:DBresODEs}. Fractional powers are obtained using the principal branch of the logarithm.  We will prove \eqref{eq:maxregdecay} in three steps.

    \emph{Step 1:}
    We first prove $L^{p_1}-L^{p_2}$ boundedness of 
    $\psi_\alpha(\tau DB)$, where by \eqref{eq:hodge}
    we  may assume that $f\in \overline{R(D)}$, since $\psi_\alpha(\tau DB) f=0$ if $f\in N(DB)$.
    Let $N>n[p_1,p_2]$ and pick a chain of
    exponents 
$$
  p_1= q_0<q_1<q_2<\ldots < q_N= p_2,
$$
where $[q_{j-1},q_j]< \frac1n$ for $j=1,2,\ldots, N$.
Estimating \eqref{eq:dunford} using
Lemma~\ref{lem:DBresODEs}\ref{it:DBODE1} gives
$$
    \nrm{\psi_{\alpha/N}(\tau DB)f}_{L^{q_j}}\lesssim
      \int_{\gamma} (\tau |\lambda|)^{\alpha/N} e^{-{c_\nu}\tau|\lambda|} |\lambda|^{n[q_{j-1},q_j]}  \frac{|\mathrm{d} \lambda|}{|\lambda|} \nrm{f}_{L^{q_{j-1}}} 
      \lesssim \tau^{-n[q_{j-1},q_j]}\nrm{f}_{L^{q_{j-1}}}, 
$$
for $j=1,\ldots, N$, with $c_\nu>0$.
Composing these operators in the functional calculus 
of $DB$ gives
\begin{align*}
   \nrm{\psi_{\alpha}(\tau DB)f}_{L^{p_2}}
   &\eqsim \nrm{\bigl(\psi_{\alpha/N}(\tfrac \tau N DB)\bigr)^N f}_{L^{p_2}} \\
&\lesssim \tau^{-n[q_{N-1},q_N]-n[q_{N-2},q_{N-1}]-\ldots -n[q_0,q_1]}
   \nrm{f}_{L^{p_1}}= \tau^{-n[p_1,p_2]}\nrm{f}_{L^{p_1}}.
\end{align*}

\emph{Step 2:}
We next prove off-diagonal estimates of 
$\psi_{\alpha}(\tau DB)$ for $E,F \subseteq \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^n$ with $d(E,F)\gtrsim \tau$ and large enough $\alpha$.
Estimating \eqref{eq:dunford} using instead
Lemma~\ref{lem:DBresODEs}\ref{item:ODEsN} gives
\begin{align*}
      \nrm{\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_F\psi_{\alpha}&(\tau DB)(f \operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_E )}_{L^{p_2}}\\
      &\lesssim
      \int_{\gamma} (\tau |\lambda|)^{\alpha} e^{-{c_\nu}\tau|\lambda|} |\lambda|^{n[p_1,p_2]}
      \bigl(|\lambda| d(E,F)\bigr)^{-(2N-1)\theta}
      e^{- c d(E,F) |\lambda|}
      \frac{|\mathrm{d} \lambda|}{|\lambda|} \nrm{f\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_E }_{L^{p_1}}\\
  &\lesssim
  \frac{\tau^\alpha d(E,F)^{-(2N-1)\theta}}
  {({c_\nu}\tau+cd(E,F))^{\alpha+n[p_1,p_2]-(2N-1)\theta}}
  \nrm{f\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_E }_{L^{p_1}}  \eqsim 
    \frac{\tau^\alpha}
  {d(E,F)^{\alpha+n[p_1,p_2]}}
  \nrm{f\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_E }_{L^{p_1}},
\end{align*}
provided that $\alpha>(2N-1)\theta-n[p_1,p_2]$.

\emph{Step 3:} Proof of \eqref{eq:maxregdecay} for $DB$.
Combining the estimates from Steps 1 and 2, we have proved that
$$
      \nrm{\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_F\psi_{\alpha}(\tau DB)(f \operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_E )}_{L^{p_2}}\lesssim
    \tau^{-n[p_1,p_2]}
    \bigl(1+d(E,F)/\tau\bigr)^{-\alpha-n[p_1,p_2]}
  \nrm{f\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_E }_{L^{p_1}},
$$
for any $E,F\subseteq \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^n$, $\tau>0$, 
and 
$\alpha>(2N-1)\theta-n[p_1,p_2]$.
By adapting the proof of \cite[Proposition 12.7]{Auscher-Egert2023-book}, we now extrapolate this 
result down to $\alpha=1$.
Using the Calder\'on reproducing formula
$$
  f= c\int_0^\infty (s\Lambda)^{\alpha-1} e^{-s\Lambda} f\frac {\mathrm{d} s}s,
$$
valid for $f\in \overline{R(DB)}\supset R(E^+)$ and $\alpha >1$,
writing $\Lambda= |DB|$ and $E^+= \operatorname{\mathbf{1}}^+(DB)$,
we get
$$
  \operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_F\tau \Lambda e^{-\tau\Lambda} E^+ (f\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_E) 
  = c\int_0^\infty \frac {\tau s^{\alpha-1}}{(s+\tau)^\alpha} \operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_F \bigl((s+\tau)\Lambda\bigr)^\alpha 
  e^{-(s+\tau)\Lambda}E^+(f \operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_E)  \frac{\mathrm{d} s}s.
$$
This gives the estimate
\begin{align*}
  \nrm{\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_F\tau \Lambda e^{-\tau\Lambda} &E^+ (f \operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_E )}_{L^{p_2}} \\
  &\lesssim \int_0^\infty \frac {\tau s^{\alpha-1}}{(s+\tau)^\alpha} 
  (s+\tau)^{-n[p_1,p_2]} 
  \bigl(1+\tfrac{d(E,F)}{s+\tau}\bigr)^{-\alpha-n[p_1,p_2]}
  \nrm{f \operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_E }_{L^{p_1}} \frac{\mathrm{d} s}s\\
  &\lesssim 
  \tau^{-n[p_1,p_2]}
  \int_0^\infty \frac {\sigma^{\alpha-1}}{(\sigma+1)^{\alpha+n[p_1,p_2]}} 
  \Bigl(1+\tfrac{d(E,F)}{\tau(\sigma+1)}\Bigr)^{-\alpha-n[p_1,p_2]}\frac{\mathrm{d} \sigma}\sigma
  \nrm{f \operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_E }_{L^{p_1}} \\
   &\lesssim 
   \tau^{-n[p_1,p_2]}\bigl(1+\tfrac{d(E,F)}\tau\bigr)^{-1-n[p_1,p_2]}
  \nrm{f \operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_E }_{L^{p_1}},
\end{align*}
where the last integral estimate with the parameter 
$d(E,F)/\tau$ is seen as in 
\cite[Proposition 12.7]{Auscher-Egert2023-book}
with $\gamma=n[p_1,p_2]$ and $\theta \alpha$
replaced by $\alpha+n[p_1,p_2]$ and choosing $\alpha$ large enough.
This proves the off-diagonal estimates \eqref{eq:maxregdecay} for $DB$, which completes the
proof.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:Jtrick}
  The operator $D\widetilde B$ on $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}$
  is similar to the direct sum of the operators
  $D_{\scriptscriptstyle \parallel} B$ and $D_{\scriptscriptstyle\perp} B$ on $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+$.
  More precisely, the isomorphism
  $J: L^r(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}; \ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}^{2+n})\to L^r(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+;\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}^{2+n})\oplus L^r(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+;\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}^{2+n})$ defined by
  $$
    (Jf)(t,x)= \frac 12
    \begin{bmatrix} f(t,x)+Rf(-t,x) \\ 
    f(t,x)-Rf(-t,x)
\end{bmatrix},\qquad t>0,
  $$
  intertwines the operators, that is, 
  $$
    \begin{bmatrix} D_{\scriptscriptstyle \parallel} B & 0 \\ 0 & D_{\scriptscriptstyle\perp} B
\end{bmatrix} J=
J (D\widetilde B)
  $$
  and $J\textsf{D}(D\widetilde B)= 
  \textsf{D}(D_{\scriptscriptstyle \parallel} B)\oplus \textsf{D}(D_{\scriptscriptstyle\perp} B)$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
One checks that 
  $\begin{bmatrix} B & 0 \\ 0 & B\end{bmatrix} J=J \widetilde B$.
  Therefore it suffices to show that
    $\begin{bmatrix} D_{\scriptscriptstyle \parallel} & 0 \\ 0 & D_{\scriptscriptstyle\perp}
\end{bmatrix} J=J D
  $.
  To this end, let $f= \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v
\end{bmatrix}$ and
$Jf= \left( \begin{bmatrix} u_+ \\ v_+
\end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} u_- \\ v_-
\end{bmatrix} \right)$.
Concretely, this means for $t>0$ that
\begin{align*}
    u_\pm(t,x)&= \tfrac 12(u(t,x)\pm u(-t,x)), \\
    v_\pm(t,x)&= \tfrac 12(v(t,x)\pm R'v(-t,x)). 
\end{align*}
The chain rule implies that 
$\nabla(u(-t,x))= R'(\nabla u)(-t,x)$
and $\operatorname{div}(R'v(-t,x))= (\operatorname{div} v)(-t,x)$.

For smooth $f$, we see that $u_-(0,x)=0= \langle v_+(0,x),e_0 \rangle$.
Conversely, if this holds, then $u$ and $\langle v,e_0 \rangle$ are continuous across $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^n$.
In general, one checks that $u\in W^{1,r}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n})$ if and only if $u_-\in W^{1,r}_0(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+)$ and
$u_+\in W^{1,r}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+)$, and also
$v\in \textsf{D}_r(\operatorname{div}_{t,x})$ on $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}$ if and only if
$v_-\in \textsf{D}_r(\operatorname{div}_{t,x})$ and
$v_+\in\textsf{D}_r(\underline{\operatorname{div}}_{t,x})$ 
on $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+$.
This shows that 
  $$
    \begin{bmatrix} D_{\scriptscriptstyle \parallel} & 0 \\ 0 & D_{\scriptscriptstyle\perp}
\end{bmatrix} J=
JD,$$
with matching domains.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:riesz}
  Let $B(t,x)$ be a bounded, measurable and accretive multiplier on $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+$.
  Let $p_\pm= p_\pm(D\widetilde B)$, $r \in (p_-,p_+)$ and  $\beta\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}$. 
  Let $p,q\in(0,\infty]$ satisfy 
  $$
n\bigl[\min\cbrace{p,q,p_-},p_-\bigr] +
    n\bigl[p_+,\max\cbrace{p,q,p_+}\bigr] < \brac{p_-,p_+}.
  $$
  Then the generalized Riesz transforms 
  $\mathrm{\mathrm{sgn}}(D_{\scriptscriptstyle \parallel} B)$ and $\mathrm{\mathrm{sgn}}(D_{\scriptscriptstyle\perp} B)$ of $\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}^{2+n}$-valued functions on 
  $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+$ are bounded on $T^{p,q,r}_\beta$
   if 
\begin{gather*}
    -\brac{p_-,q}+n\bigl[\min\cbrace{p,q,p_-},p_-\bigr]<\beta<\brac{q,p_+}-n\bigl[p_+,\max\cbrace{p,q,p_+}\bigr].
\end{gather*}
The same result holds for the Riesz transforms $R_{N,A}$ and $R_{D,A}$, mapping $\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}$-valued functions to $\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}^{1+n}$-valued
functions, in \eqref{eq:RTNeu} and \eqref{eq:RTDir} with $p_\pm(D\widetilde B)$ replaced by 
$q_\pm(\tilde L)$.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
Let $p_-(D\widetilde B)<p_1<r<p_2<p_+(D\widetilde B)$ and note that the operator $D\widetilde B$ on $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}$ from 
  Lemma~\ref{lem:Jtrick} has a bounded $H^\infty$ functional calculus in $L^r(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n};\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}^{2+n})$.
    Consider first the auxiliary generalized Riesz transform $S=\mathrm{sgn}(D\widetilde B)$, which is bounded on $L^r(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n};\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}^{2+n})$.
    To prove off-diagonal estimates for $S$, by functional calculus we have
    $$
      \mathrm{sgn}(D\widetilde B)= c_N\int_0^\infty
      \psi(\tau D\widetilde B) \ \frac{\mathrm{d} \tau}\tau,
    $$
    where $\psi(\lambda)= \lambda^N/(1+\lambda^2)^N$ for odd $N\in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$  and
    $0<c_N<\infty$.
    From Lemma~\ref{lem:DBresODEs} in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}$ and 
    \cite[Lemma 4.6]{Auscher-Egert2023-book}, we have
    $$
\|\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_{\boldsymbol{\widetilde F}} \psi(\tau D\widetilde B) (f \operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_{\boldsymbol{\widetilde E}} )\|_{L^{p_2}_{t,x}}\le 
C \tau^{-(n+1)[p_1,p_2]} e^{- c d(\boldsymbol{\widetilde E} , \boldsymbol{\widetilde F})/\tau}
\|\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_{\boldsymbol{\widetilde E}}f \|_{L^{p_1}_{t,x}}
$$
for subsets $\boldsymbol{\widetilde E},\boldsymbol{\widetilde F}\subset \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}$
and some $c>0$, and $N>(n+1)[p_1,p_2]$
which we fix.
We get
\begin{align*}
\|\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_{\boldsymbol{\widetilde F}} \mathrm{sgn}(D\widetilde B) ( f\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_{\boldsymbol{\widetilde E}} )\|_{L^{p_2}_{t,x}}
&\lesssim \int_0^\infty  \tau^{-(n+1)[p_1,p_2]} 
e^{- c d(\boldsymbol{\widetilde E} , \boldsymbol{\widetilde F})/\tau}
\|f \operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_{\boldsymbol{\widetilde E}}\|_{L^{p_1}_{t,x}}
\frac{\hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} \tau}\tau \\
&\lesssim d(\boldsymbol{\widetilde E},\boldsymbol{\widetilde F})^{-(n+1)[p_1,p_2]}
\|f \operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_{\boldsymbol{\widetilde E}}\|_{L^{p_1}_{t,x}}.
\end{align*}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:Jtrick}, the same off-diagonal
estimates for subsets $\boldsymbol{E},\boldsymbol{F}$ of $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}_+$ hold for 
$\mathrm{sgn}(D_{\scriptscriptstyle \parallel} B)$ and $\mathrm{sgn}(D_{\scriptscriptstyle\perp} B)$,
since
  $$
    \begin{bmatrix} \mathrm{sgn}(D_{\scriptscriptstyle \parallel} B) & 0 \\ 0 & \mathrm{sgn}(D_{\scriptscriptstyle\perp} B)
\end{bmatrix} J=
J \,\mathrm{sgn}(D\widetilde B),
  $$
and noting that  we have 
$d(\boldsymbol{\widetilde E}, \boldsymbol{\widetilde F})= d(\boldsymbol{E},\boldsymbol{F})$,
where $\boldsymbol{\widetilde E}= \boldsymbol{E}\cup R'\boldsymbol{E}$ and
$\boldsymbol{\widetilde F}= \boldsymbol{F}\cup R'\boldsymbol{F}$,
acting pointwise with the reflection $R'$ on the sets. 

We have therefore shown \eqref{eq:odeprototype} with $M=0$, $m=1$, $\kappa=0$,  $(u_t,u_x)=(p_1,p_1)$ and $(v_t,v_x)=(p_2,p_2)$.  Proposition~\ref{prop:SIO-simple} 
applies to show  that $\mathrm{sgn}(D_{\scriptscriptstyle \parallel} B)$ and $\mathrm{sgn}(D_{\scriptscriptstyle\perp} B)$ are singular operators of type $(0,1,r,(p_1,p_1),(p_2,p_2),0)$ in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:ODE}.
Their tent space bounds now follow from Theorem~\ref{thm:mainestimate},
if $p_1,p_2$ are such that
\begin{align*}
    n\bigl[\min\cbrace{p,q,p_1},p_1\bigr] +
    n\bigl[p_2,\max\cbrace{p,q,p_2}\bigr] < \brac{p_1,p_2}
\end{align*}
and
\begin{align*}
-\brac{p_1,q}+n\bigl[\min\cbrace{p,q,p_1},p_1\bigr]<\beta<\brac{q,p_2}-n\bigl[p_2,\max\cbrace{p,q,p_2}\bigr].
\end{align*}
Since $p_1>p_-(D\widetilde B)$ and $p_2<p_+(D\widetilde B)$ are arbitrary,
the result for $\mathrm{\mathrm{sgn}}(D_{\scriptscriptstyle \parallel} B)$ and $\mathrm{\mathrm{sgn}}(D_{\scriptscriptstyle\perp} B)$ follows.

The result for the Riesz transforms 
$R_{N,A}$ and $R_{D,A}$
is proved analogously, replacing $p_\pm(D\widetilde B)$ by 
$q_\pm(\tilde L)$, the endpoints of the maximal interval on which the Riesz transform $\nabla \tilde L^{-1/2}$ is $L^p$-bounded. See \cite[Theorem~7.3]{Auscher-Egert2023-book}.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- prop-12: body_md -->
\label{prop:Vrho,p}
    Let $q,p \in (1,\infty)$.
    \begin{enumerate}[label=\normalfont(\roman*)]
        \item \label{item:Vrho,p-eq-norms}
        {\normalfont (Equivalent norms)}
        It holds that
        \begin{align*}
            \|f\|_{\dot\cV^{q,p}} &\eqsim \|\nabla_x f\|_{ 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{q}\smash[d]{p}}\smash[d]{q}}_{\vphantom{tx}t} 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{q}\smash[d]{p}}\smash[d]{p}}_{\vphantom{tx}x} 
} + \|D_t^{1/2}f\|_{ 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{q}\smash[d]{p}}\smash[d]{q}}_{\vphantom{tx}t} 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{q}\smash[d]{p}}\smash[d]{p}}_{\vphantom{tx}x} 
}, && f \in \dot\cV^{q,p}, \\
            \|f\|_{\cV^{q,p}} &\eqsim \|f\|_{ 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{q}\smash[d]{p}}\smash[d]{q}}_{\vphantom{tx}t} 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{q}\smash[d]{p}}\smash[d]{p}}_{\vphantom{tx}x} 
} + \|\nabla_x f\|_{ 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{q}\smash[d]{p}}\smash[d]{q}}_{\vphantom{tx}t} 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{q}\smash[d]{p}}\smash[d]{p}}_{\vphantom{tx}x} 
} + \|D_t^{1/2}f\|_{ 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{q}\smash[d]{p}}\smash[d]{q}}_{\vphantom{tx}t} 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{q}\smash[d]{p}}\smash[d]{p}}_{\vphantom{tx}x} 
}, && f \in \cV^{q,p}.
        \end{align*}
        
        \item \label{item:Vrho,p-Sobolev-embed}
        {\normalfont (Sobolev embedding)}
        The space $\dot\cV^{q,p}$ embeds into $ 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{\ovq}\smash[d]{\ovp}}\smash[d]{\ovq}}_{\vphantom{tx}t} 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{\ovq}\smash[d]{\ovp}}\smash[d]{\ovp}}_{\vphantom{tx}x} 
$ if
        \begin{equation}
            \label{eq:parabolicembedding}
            2[q,\ovq]+n[p,\ovp]=1, \quad (\ovq,\ovp)\in [q,\infty) \times [p,\infty). 
        \end{equation}
        The space $\cV^{q,p}$ embeds into $ 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{\ovq}\smash[d]{\ovp}}\smash[d]{\ovq}}_{\vphantom{tx}t} 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{\ovq}\smash[d]{\ovp}}\smash[d]{\ovp}}_{\vphantom{tx}x} 
$ if
        \begin{equation}
            \label{eq:parabolicembeddinginhomogeneous}
            2[q,\ovq]+n[p,\ovp]\le 1,  \quad (\ovq,\ovp)\in [q,\infty)\times [p,\infty). 
        \end{equation}
        Moreover, assume $q>2$. Then the space $\cV^{q,p}$ embeds into $ 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{\infty}\smash[d]{\ovp}}\smash[d]{\infty}}_{\vphantom{tx}t} 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{\infty}\smash[d]{\ovp}}\smash[d]{\ovp}}_{\vphantom{tx}x} 
$ if 
        \begin{equation}\label{eq:parabolicembeddinginfty}
            \begin{cases}
            \ovp\in  [p,\infty]   &\text{if}\ \  2[q,\infty]+n[p,\infty] < 1 \\
            \ovp\in  [p,\infty)   &\text{if}\ \ 2[q,\infty]+n[p,\infty] = 1 \\
            \ovp\in  [p,\frac{n}{2[q,\infty]+n[p,\infty]-1})   &\text{if}\ \  2[q,\infty]+n[p,\infty] > 1.
        \end{cases}
        \end{equation}
    \end{enumerate}
    All the implicit constants depend only on $n, q, p, \ovq, \ovp$.
<!-- end prop-12 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
We only present the proof in the homogeneous case. The inhomogeneous counterparts follow similarly. The reader can also refer to \cite[Theorem 1.1]{Li21} and \cite[Theorem 7]{Johnsen-Sickel2007-mixed-Sobolev-embedding} for the proof. By density, it suffices to prove these two statements for $f \in \cZ(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n})$. Define $g \in \cZ(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n})$ by the Fourier multiplication $\hatg(\tau,\xi) := |(\tau,\xi)|_{\mathrm{par}} \hatf(\tau,\xi)$. Define $\tilde \psi \in \cZ(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n})$ by $\hat{\tilde\psi}(\tau,\xi) := |(\tau,\xi)|_{\mathrm{par}}^{-1} \hat\psi(\tau,\xi)$. Then we infer that
    \[ \|g\|_{ 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{q}\smash[d]{p}}\smash[d]{q}}_{\vphantom{tx}t} 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{q}\smash[d]{p}}\smash[d]{p}}_{\vphantom{tx}x} 
} \eqsim \bigl\| \|(\tilde\psi_j\ast g)_{j\in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}}\|_{\ell^2(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}})} \bigr\|_{ 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{q}\smash[d]{p}}\smash[d]{q}}_{\vphantom{tx}t} 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{q}\smash[d]{p}}\smash[d]{p}}_{\vphantom{tx}x} 
} = \bigl\| \|(2^j\psi_j\ast f)_{j\in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}} \|_{\ell^2(\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}})} \bigr\|_{ 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{q}\smash[d]{p}}\smash[d]{q}}_{\vphantom{tx}t} 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{q}\smash[d]{p}}\smash[d]{p}}_{\vphantom{tx}x} 
} = \|f\|_{\dot\cV^{q,p}}. \]

    Let us prove \ref{item:Vrho,p-eq-norms}. Note that
    \[ (|\tau|^{1/2} + |\xi|) \hatf (\tau,\xi) = \frac{|\tau|^{1/2}+|\xi|}{|(\tau,\xi)|_{\mathrm{par}}} |(\tau,\xi)|_{\mathrm{par}} \hatf(\tau,\xi) = \frac{|\tau|^{1/2}+|\xi|}{|(\tau,\xi)|_{\mathrm{par}}} \hatg(\tau,\xi). \]
    The symbol $m(\tau,\xi) := \frac{|\tau|^{1/2}+|\xi|}{|(\tau,\xi)|_{\mathrm{par}}}$ satisfies Mikhlin's condition $| |\tau|^{\alpha} |\xi|^{|\beta|} \partial^{\alpha}_\tau \partial_\xi^\beta m(\tau,\xi) | \le C(\alpha,\beta) < \infty$ for all $\alpha \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$ and multi-indices $\beta \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}^n$. Hence, the Mikhlin (or Marcinkiewicz) multiplier theorem in mixed-norm Lebesgue spaces (see \cite{Liz70}) shows that
    \[ \|D_t^{1/2} f\|_{ 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{q}\smash[d]{p}}\smash[d]{q}}_{\vphantom{tx}t} 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{q}\smash[d]{p}}\smash[d]{p}}_{\vphantom{tx}x} 
} + \|\nabla_x f\|_{ 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{q}\smash[d]{p}}\smash[d]{q}}_{\vphantom{tx}t} 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{q}\smash[d]{p}}\smash[d]{p}}_{\vphantom{tx}x} 
} \lesssim \|g\|_{ 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{q}\smash[d]{p}}\smash[d]{q}}_{\vphantom{tx}t} 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{q}\smash[d]{p}}\smash[d]{p}}_{\vphantom{tx}x} 
} \eqsim \|f\|_{\dot\cV^{q,p}}. \]
    Applying the same reasoning to $1/m$ gives us the reverse inequality. This proves \ref{item:Vrho,p-eq-norms}.

    Next, we prove \ref{item:Vrho,p-Sobolev-embed}. Observe that if $2[q,\infty]+n[p,\infty] \le 1$, then there do not exist such $\ovq$ and $\ovp$ satisfying \eqref{eq:parabolicembedding}. So assume $2[q,\infty]+n[p,\infty] > 1$. In this case, $\dot\cV^{q,p}$ embeds into $\cS'(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n})$. Pick $\theta=2[q,\ovq]$, so that $\theta \in [0,2/q)$ and $1-\theta= n[p,\ovp]$ upon \eqref{eq:parabolicembedding}. Write
    \[ \hat f(\tau, \xi) = \frac{|\tau|^{\theta/2}|\xi|^{1-\theta}}{| (\tau,\xi) |_{\mathrm{par}}} |\tau|^{-\theta/2}|\xi|^{-1+\theta} \hat g(\tau, \xi). \]
    The symbol $\frac{|\tau|^{\theta/2}|\xi|^{1-\theta}}{| (\tau,\xi) |_{\mathrm{par}}}$ also satisfies Mikhlin's condition. Thus, using the Mikhlin multiplier theorem and boundedness of the Riesz potentials, we get
    \[ \|f\|_{ 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{\ovq}\smash[d]{\ovp}}\smash[d]{\ovq}}_{\vphantom{tx}t} 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{\ovq}\smash[d]{\ovp}}\smash[d]{\ovp}}_{\vphantom{tx}x} 
} \lesssim \|(|\tau|^{-\theta/2} |\xi|^{-1+\theta} \hat g)^\vee \|_{ 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{\ovq}\smash[d]{\ovp}}\smash[d]{\ovq}}_{\vphantom{tx}t} 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{\ovq}\smash[d]{\ovp}}\smash[d]{\ovp}}_{\vphantom{tx}x} 
} \lesssim \|( |\xi|^{-1+\theta} \hat g)^\vee \|_{ 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{q}\smash[d]{\ovp}}\smash[d]{q}}_{\vphantom{tx}t} 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{q}\smash[d]{\ovp}}\smash[d]{\ovp}}_{\vphantom{tx}x} 
} \lesssim \|g\|_{  
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{q}\smash[d]{p}}\smash[d]{q}}_{\vphantom{tx}t} 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{q}\smash[d]{p}}\smash[d]{p}}_{\vphantom{tx}x} 
 } \eqsim \|f\|_{\dot\cV^{q,p}}. \]
    The second inequality can be proved for example using representation in space variables of the Riesz potential in the $t$-variable and Minkowski integral inequality. This proves \ref{item:Vrho,p-Sobolev-embed} and completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- prop-13: body_md -->
\label{prop:sneiberg}
    There exists $\varepsilon>0$ such that if $q,p \in (1,\infty)$ satisfy $|[2,q]|<\varepsilon$ and $|[2,p]|<\varepsilon$, we have bounded extensions
    \begin{equation}
        \label{eq:homSneiberg}
        (\pm \partial_t - \operatorname{div}_x(A(t,x)\nabla_x))^{-1} \colon (\dot\cV^{q',p'})' \to \dot\cV^{q,p}
    \end{equation}
    and 
    \begin{equation}
        \label{eq:inhomSneiberg} 
        (\pm \partial_t - \operatorname{div}_x(A(t,x)\nabla_x)+1)^{-1} \colon (\cV^{q',p'})' \to \cV^{q,p}.
    \end{equation}
<!-- end prop-13 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{def:v(A)}
    Let $(v_-(A),v_+(A)) \subset (1,\infty)$ be the largest open interval for which \eqref{eq:homSneiberg} and \eqref{eq:inhomSneiberg} hold for all $q,p\in (v_-(A),v_+(A))$.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
The inhomogeneous counterpart \eqref{eq:inhomSneiberg} has been established in \cite[Section 6.1]{AEN20} via Sneiberg's extrapolation lemma. See also the appendix of \cite{ABES19a} for a proof of the quantitative version of Sneiberg's lemma justifying the use of two parameters in the extrapolation. The same argument applies to the homogeneous result \eqref{eq:homSneiberg}, where we first pass in the target to the quotient spaces $(\dot\cV^{q,p}+\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}})/\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}$  which form  a scale of complex interpolation Banach spaces and then conclude by lifting.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- remark-20: body_md -->
In the case where $A$ is the identity matrix $\bfI$, we have $v_-(\bfI)=1$ and $v_+(\bfI)=\infty$. Indeed, it amounts to proving the $ 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{q}\smash[d]{p}}\smash[d]{q}}_{\vphantom{tx}t} 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{q}\smash[d]{p}}\smash[d]{p}}_{\vphantom{tx}x} 
$ boundedness of the Fourier multipliers $\frac{(|\tau|^2+|\xi|^4)^{1/2}}{\pm i\tau + |\xi|^2} $ and $\frac{(|\tau|^2+|\xi|^4+1)^{1/2}}{\pm i\tau + |\xi|^2+1}$, which again follows from the Mikhlin multiplier theorem. It would be interesting to investigate the precise values of these critical exponents when $A$ has some regularity, e.g., when $x \mapsto A(t,x)$ belongs to $VMO$, to connect with   \cite{Krylov2007-para-ell-VMO,Krylov2007-parabolic-VMO,Dong-Kim2011-system-BMO}. We leave that to further developments.
<!-- end remark-20 -->
<!-- cor-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:para-op-mixed-Leb}
    Let $q,p \in (v_-(A),v_+(A))$. Let $\ovq \in [q,\infty)$ and $\ovp \in [p,\infty)$ with $2[q,\ovq]+n[p,\ovp] = 1$. Let $\ulq \in (1,q]$ and $\ulp \in (1,p]$ with $2[\ulq,q]+n[\ulp,p]=1$. Then
    \begin{align*}
        \nabla_x (\pm \partial_t - \operatorname{div}_x(A(t,x)\nabla_x))^{-1}\operatorname{div}_x &\colon  
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{q}\smash[d]{p}}\smash[d]{q}}_{\vphantom{tx}t} 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{q}\smash[d]{p}}\smash[d]{p}}_{\vphantom{tx}x} 
 \to  
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{q}\smash[d]{p}}\smash[d]{q}}_{\vphantom{tx}t} 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{q}\smash[d]{p}}\smash[d]{p}}_{\vphantom{tx}x} 
 \\
        (\pm \partial_t - \operatorname{div}_x(A(t,x)\nabla_x))^{-1}\operatorname{div}_x &\colon  
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{q}\smash[d]{p}}\smash[d]{q}}_{\vphantom{tx}t} 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{q}\smash[d]{p}}\smash[d]{p}}_{\vphantom{tx}x} 
 \to  
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{\ovq}\smash[d]{\ovp}}\smash[d]{\ovq}}_{\vphantom{tx}t} 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{\ovq}\smash[d]{\ovp}}\smash[d]{\ovp}}_{\vphantom{tx}x} 
 \\
        \nabla_x (\pm \partial_t - \operatorname{div}_x(A(t,x)\nabla_x))^{-1} &\colon  
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{\ulq}\smash[d]{\ulp}}\smash[d]{\ulq}}_{\vphantom{tx}t} 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{\ulq}\smash[d]{\ulp}}\smash[d]{\ulp}}_{\vphantom{tx}x} 
 \to  
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{q}\smash[d]{p}}\smash[d]{q}}_{\vphantom{tx}t} 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{q}\smash[d]{p}}\smash[d]{p}}_{\vphantom{tx}x} 
 \\
        (\pm \partial_t - \operatorname{div}_x(A(t,x)\nabla_x))^{-1} &\colon  
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{\ulq}\smash[d]{\ulp}}\smash[d]{\ulq}}_{\vphantom{tx}t} 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{\ulq}\smash[d]{\ulp}}\smash[d]{\ulp}}_{\vphantom{tx}x} 
 \to  
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{\ovq}\smash[d]{\ovp}}\smash[d]{\ovq}}_{\vphantom{tx}t} 
  L^{\vphantom{\smash[d]{\ovq}\smash[d]{\ovp}}\smash[d]{\ovp}}_{\vphantom{tx}x} 
.
    \end{align*}
    For the operators $(\pm \partial_t - \operatorname{div}_x(A(t,x)\nabla_x)+1)^{-1}$, the same statements hold with the modifications $2[q,\ovq]+n[p,\ovp] \le 1$ and $2[\ulq,q]+n[\ulp,p] \le 1$.
<!-- end cor-2 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
To prove the first boundedness, we first infer from Proposition \ref{prop:Vrho,p}\ref{item:Vrho,p-eq-norms} that $L^{\vphantom{-1,p}q}_t \dot{H}^{-1,p}_{\vphantom{t}x}$ embeds into $(\dot\cV^{q',p'})'$ and $\dot\cV^{q,p}$ embeds into $L^{\vphantom{-1,p}q}_t \dot{H}^{1,p}_{\vphantom{t}x}$. Then it directly follows from \eqref{eq:homSneiberg}.
    Then the three others follow on applying the embeddings and duality, noting that the same argument applies to the adjoints $(\mp \partial_t - \operatorname{div}_x(A^*(t,x)\nabla_x))^{-1}$ in parallel. The proof for the inhomogeneous case is similar.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- prop-14: body_md -->
\label{prop:rhi} 
    Let $I \times B$ with $|I| \eqsim r(B)^2$ be a parabolic cylinder and $u \in L^2(\gamma^2 I; H^1(\gamma B))$ be a weak solution to $\partial_t u - \operatorname{div}_x(A(t,x)\nabla_x u)=0$ on $\gamma^2 I \times \gamma B$ for some $\gamma>1$. Let $1<\delta<\gamma$.
    For $0 < p < v_+(A)$, we have
    \begin{equation}
        \label{eq:p-Caccioppoli1}
        \int_{I}\int_{B} |\nabla u(s,y)|^p \hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} y \hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} s \lesssim r(B)^{-p} \int_{\delta^2 I}\int_{\delta B} |u(s,y)|^p \hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} y \hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} s.
    \end{equation} 
    For $0< \ovp<\ v_+(A)^\sharp$ if $v_+(A)\le n+2$ and $0< \ovp \le \infty$ otherwise, we have
    \begin{equation}
        \label{eq:RHIu}
        \sup_{s \in I} \bigg(\fint_{B} |u(s,y)|^{\ovp} \hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} y \bigg)^{1/\ovp}  \lesssim \bigg(\fint_{\delta^2 I} \fint_{\delta B} |u(s,y)|^2 \hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} y \hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} s\bigg)^{1/2},
    \end{equation}
    and 
    \begin{equation}
        \label{eq:RHIuq}
        \bigg(\fint_{I}\fint_{B} | u(s,y)|^{\ovp} \hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} y\hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} s\bigg)^{1/\ovp}  \lesssim  \fint_{\delta^2 I}\fint_{\delta B} |u(s,y)| \hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} y \hspace{2pt}\mathrm{d} s
    \end{equation}
    with the canonical modification if $\ovp=\infty$. The implicit constants do not depend on $I, B$. The Euclidean balls on $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^n$ can be replaced by cubes. The same statement holds for weak solutions of the backward equation $-\partial_t u - \operatorname{div}_x(A(t,x)\nabla_x u)=0$.
<!-- end prop-14 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
Let us first prove the intermediate estimate
\begin{equation}
    \label{e:para-RH-intermediate}
    \| u\chi\|_{\cV^{p,p}} \lesssim \|u\tilde \chi\|_{L^2_{t,x}}
\end{equation}
for any $2\le p<v_+(A)$, assuming $I$  interval of length 1, $B$ ball of radius $r(B)\eqsim 1$, and $\chi,\tilde \chi$ two smooth functions with $\operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_{I \times B} \le \chi \le \tilde \chi \le \operatorname{\mathbf{1}}_{\gamma^2 I \times \gamma B}$, the implicit constant being independent of $I$ and $B$. To this end, let $\chi_i$, $i=1, 2, \ldots, 2k+2$, for some $k$ to be determined, be smooth functions supported in $\gamma_i^2 I \times \gamma_i B$ with $1<\gamma_i<\gamma$ and $\chi_{i+1}=1$ on this support. Write $v_i \coloneq \chi_i u$. Since $v_i$ is compactly supported, we may use H\"older's inequality freely. Then     
\begin{equation}
    \label{e:para-local-vi}
    \partial_t v_i - \operatorname{div}_x(A(t,x)\nabla_x v_i) +v_i=  f_i+\operatorname{div}_x F_{i}
\end{equation}
on $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{1+n}$, in the weak sense, with $f_i= (\partial_t\chi_i +\chi_i) v_{i+1} -A \nabla_x v_{i+1}\cdot \nabla_x \chi_i$ and $F_i=-A (v_{i+1}\nabla_x \chi_i)$ using the support assumptions. As $f_i \in L^{2_\ast}_{t,x}$, $F_i \in L^2_{t,x}$, and $v_i \in L^{2}_t H^1_{\vphantom{t}x}$, we invoke \cite[Proposition 3.1]{Auscher-Bortz-Egert-Saari2019-parabolicL2} to get $D_t^{1/2}v_i\in L^2_{t,x}$ and hence $v_i \in \cV^{2,2}$. Furthermore, we infer from existence and uniqueness of weak solutions to \eqref{e:para-local-vi} in $\cV^{2,2}$ (see \cite{AE23}) that
\[ v_i = (\partial_t - \operatorname{div}_x(A(t,x)\nabla_x)+1)^{-1} (f_i+\operatorname{div}_x F_{i}). \]
For $2 \le p < v_+(A)$, given $p_1 \in [2,p]$ with $(2+n)[p_1,p] = (2+n)[p',p_1'] \le 1$, the Sobolev embedding (cf. Proposition \ref{prop:Vrho,p}\ref{item:Vrho,p-Sobolev-embed}) yields that $\cV^{p_1,p_1} \hookrightarrow L^p_{t,x}$, $\cV^{p',p'} \hookrightarrow L^{p_1'}_{t,x}$, and hence $L^{p_1}_{t,x} \hookrightarrow (\cV^{p',p'})'$. We also get from Proposition \ref{prop:Vrho,p}\ref{item:Vrho,p-eq-norms} that $L^{\vphantom{-1,p}p}_t \dot{H}^{-1,p}_{\vphantom{t}x} \hookrightarrow (\cV^{p',p'})'$. So we have
\[ \|v_i\|_{\cV^{p,p}} \lesssim \|f_i\|_{L^{p_1}_{t,x}} + \|F_i\|_{L^p_{t,x}} \lesssim  \|\nabla_x v_{i+1}\|_{L^{p_1}_{t,x}} + \|v_{i+1}\|_{L^p_{t,x}}. \]
